  114. the first principles
    of life must be "tender and ductile"     Thomas Burnet, The Theory of the Earth (The Sacred Theory of the Earth) Brass (1971) · The Kirghiz Disasters · l.5561 · p.158 · new/high

    English version, 1684/1691, Book II ch. 2; reprinted with an introduction by Basil Willey (London: Centaur Press, 1965); quoted in the OED s.v. 'ductile' as 'Burnet Th. Earth I. 187'; Book II, ch. 2 ('Concerning the Primaeval Earth and Paradise') source ↗

    The first principles of life must be tender and ductile, that they may yield to all the motions and gentle touches of Nature; otherwise it is not possible that they should be wrought with that curiosity ...

    Burnet's sentence concerns the antediluvian 'primigenial soil', which was soft enough to breed animals before the Flood fixed the earth in its ruined, mountainous form. In a poem full of ice, fallen rock, 'jurassic boredom' and 'liassic beds', Prynne applies it to a dental technician's new bridge-work. Prelapsarian ductility becomes the softness of dentures, and 'strip off, and / that too is rotten' completes Burnet's fall from tender origins into a decayed present. The phrase may have reached Prynne through the OED, which quotes it under 'ductile'.

'Thomas Burnet' is mentioned (Luker 2017; Roebuck and Sperling on 'The Glacial Question, Unsolved') only for other poems.   115. You sleep on, seeded by snowy drift. George Woodcock and Ivan Avakumović, The Doukhobors Brass (1971) · Royal Fern · l.5581 · p.2 · new/medium

    His victims are also celebrated, their sufferings and courage woven into the Doukhobor consciousness.     The shared words are only 'Sleep on, you', inverted to 'You sleep on'. The claim rests on position: the same page of Woodcock gives the hymn title that opens stanza 3 ('In his youth he walked much'), so stanza 1 most probably draws on the other hymn named there. The Doukhobor hymn is sung to the sect's dead, the victims of persecution and exile. Prynne's sleeper 'seeded by snowy drift' is then a buried martyr under Russian or Canadian snow, and 'seeded' carries the hymn's promise of resurrection. This colours the poem's dream-love ('How can you love me in dream, / always walking from field to field') with the sect's wandering and its graves. It also prepares 'Still the snow hums' and 'the key' of stanza 4, which recalls Danilo's lost 'church keys' on the same page. A companion to the hymn entry at l. 5590 (same Woodcock leaf, 'Sleep on, you brave fighting eagles'); stanza 3's 'staring the wing blind' may answer the hymn's 'eagles'.

The hymn's fuller text ('Sleep on, you brave fighting eagles, / Sleep on in the arms of the Lord') is in The Doukhobors of British Columbia (1955), seen on IA.

The following stanza's 'still the key / takes cover in the chamois case. / The key is the edge of our day' then reads as the church keys lost with the golden book. The poem's sleeping wanderer 'laden with scrip', 'always walking from field to field', takes on the Doukhobor pilgrim.   118. the fire
    of heaven, gentle, very light. ... What is
    this high street at night, in every direction the
    same as itself?     Parmenides, tr. John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy Brass (1971) · The Five Hindrances · l.5720 · p.163 · known/high

    3rd ed., London: A. & C. Black, 1920; fr. 8, p. 176 source ↗

    They have distinguished them as opposite in form, and have assigned to them marks distinct from one another. To the one they allot the fire of heaven, gentle, very light, in every direction the same as itself, but not the same as the other. The other is just the opposite to it, dark night, a compact and heavy body.

    Prynne splits Burnet's sentence across five lines. He gives the light form ('the fire / of heaven, gentle, very light') to the pilot-light of a gas mantle ('The brilliant patch / (thorium)'), and he gives its self-identity ('in every direction the / same as itself') to a 'high street at night', which in Parmenides is the opposite form. The irony is exact: mortal opinion names light and night as two, and the poem hands the attribute of the one to a scene of the other. The poem then asks whether the urban night 'will not change'. The next line, 'pleads for its topical centre', recalls fr.12 (the goddess 'driving the female to the embrace of the male'), both on p. 177.

    quotation. Sutherland, 'Hilarious absolute daybreak', Glossator 2 (2010).

    Verified: Read in the djvu text of earlygreekphilos00burnrich (p. 176). An automatic 4-gram match of ll. 5240-5740 against this text gives 'the fire of heaven gentle', 'heaven gentle very light' and 'in every direction the same as itself' only at ll. 5720-5726. inside.py also finds the wording in McClure (1935) and the Philosophical Review (1943), which reprint Burnet.

  119. at the tiny rate of say 0.25 per cent

    Prynne's 'say 0.25' takes the midpoint of Fogg's range ('between 0.2 and 0.3'), and the inner quotation marks keep Fogg's own phrase. The 'tiny rate' is the real yield of the Earthrise planet, and a primer's scientific neutrality presents it as a providential economy.

Snippets read inside both IA scans (photosynthesis00fogg, photosynthesis00gefo) and an unattributed scan (photosynthesis0000unse); olinside.py identifies author and publisher.   120. the total crop yield
    of fear, from the fixation of danger; in
    how we are gripped in the dark, the
    flashes of where we are ... the stable end-product is dark
    motion, glints of terror the final inert
    residue. Oriental human beings throw off
    their leafy canopies ... The
    photochemical dispatch is imminent ... The
    permeated spectra of hatred dominate
    all the wavebands, algal to hominid.     G. E. Fogg, Photosynthesis Brass (1971) · The Ideal Star-Fighter · l.5786 · p.165 · partial/medium

    London: English Universities Press, 1968; ch. 5, 'The path of carbon assimilation' (contents p. 61: 'Dark fixation of carbon dioxide'; 'The formation of PGA'); the sections on intermittent light (fig. 38) and on the leaf canopy; absorption spectra (figs. 7, 8, 18) source ↗

    Dark fixation of carbon dioxide [section title] | [PGA was] quickly recognized as being the first stable product of photosynthetic carbon fixation | the photosynthetic yield from a given amount of light is greater if it is given in short intense flashes separated by dark periods than if it is given ... | later the leaf canopy only reaches maximum photosynthetic efficiency for a week or ... | photochemical reactions | algal cells | Absorption spectra of bacteriochlorophyll, chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b

    The 0.25 per cent quotation is not isolated. The first part of the poem keeps to the technical lexicon of Fogg's primer: 'yield', 'fixation' (carbon fixation, and Fogg's 'dark fixation'), the light 'flashes' separated by dark periods, the 'stable end-product' (Fogg's 'first stable product of photosynthetic carbon fixation'), the 'leafy canopies', and in part III 'photochemical', 'spectra' and 'algal'. Fear takes the place of carbon in the process: fear is fixed from danger in the dark, and its stable product is 'dark motion' and an 'inert residue', not sugar. So the 'switchboard of organic providence' is a real metabolic chain, and terror is its end-product. The 'leafy canopies' that 'Oriental human beings throw off' put the My Lai charge-sheet phrase into the same plant-physiological register. Fogg's 'the total yield of photosynthesis', in the same section as the 0.25 per cent quotation (l. 5782), stands behind 'total crop yield'.

    adaptation. The first pass found Fogg only for the 0.25 per cent quotation. kbgrep 'Fogg', 'stable product', 'inert residue': no critic names Fogg. Pietrzak (bib-9a5bd81a75) and Luna (Critical Inquiry 2016) read 'the fixation of danger' and 'gripped in the dark' as existential and ecological figures, without the photosynthetic sense.

  122. Oriental human beings throw off
    their leafy canopies, expire     United States Army (charge sheet against 1st Lt William L. Calley, Jr.), Specifications of murder at My Lai 4 (Art. 118, UCMJ) Brass (1971) · The Ideal Star-Fighter · l.5797 · p.165 · new/high

    preferred 5 Sept. 1969; text widely printed in the press from 24 Nov. 1969 (e.g. Lompoc Record, Dixon Evening Telegraph); verdict 29 Mar. 1971; Specifications 1-4; reprinted in Everett, Johnson and Rosenthal, Calley (1971) source ↗

    did, at My Lai 4, ... with premeditation, murder an unknown number, not less than 30, Oriental human beings, males and females of various ages, whose names are unknown, occupants of the village of My Lai 4 ... murder an unknown number of Oriental human beings, not less than 70

    The phrase is not Prynne's euphemism. It is the US Army's legal formula for the My Lai dead, which every newspaper repeated from November 1969. Prynne joins it to the defoliation image ('throw off their leafy canopies, expire'). The court-martial's bureaucratic racial category and the chemical war on the forest canopy become one sentence. The judicial abstraction that names the victims only as a class is the poem's 'moral pigment of these times'.

    quotation. kbgrep 'Oriental human', 'Calley', 'My Lai': Luna (2016) reads the line as napalm and Agent Orange, with 'facetiously euphemistic vocabulary'. Luker (2017) reads it as a guerrilla seen on television. Neither identifies the court-martial formula.

    Verified: inside.py 'Oriental human beings' (<1972): of 75 hits, almost all from 1969-71 are reports of the Calley charges. Snippets seen in Lompoc Record 24 Nov. 1969 and in Calley (1971). The 1937 'Representative American speeches' hit is a misdated later volume quoting the charges.

  125. death hovers because of
    the dove's lamentation, his part of the soul.     Ibn al-'Arabi, trans. Reynold A. Nicholson, The Tarjumán al-Ashwáq: A Collection of Mystical Odes (Oriental Translation Fund, n.s. XX) Brass (1971) · Nothing Like Examples (Brass) · l.5866 · p.167 · new/high

    London: Royal Asiatic Society, 1911; ode quoted again in Rom Landau, The Philosophy of Ibn 'Arabi (London: Allen & Unwin, 1959); also reprinted in Landau, The Philosophy of Ibn 'Arabi (1959); Ode XVI, verse 10, p. 78; commentary pp. 79-80 source ↗

    7. O dove of the arák trees, have a little pity on me! for parting only increased thy moans, 8. And thy lamentation, O dove, inflames the longing lover, excites the jealous, 9. Melts the heart, drives off sleep, and doubles our desires and sighing. 10. Death hovers because of the dove's lamentation, and we beg him to spare us a little while ... COMMENTARY ... 7. 'O dove of the arák trees': he addresses holy influences of Divine pleasure which have descended upon him ... 'Inasmuch as thy substance only exists through and in me ...' ... 10. 'Death,' i.e. the station in which the subtle principle of Man is severed from its governance of this dark body

    One whole clause of Ibn 'Arabi's love ode is set without marks into a stanza of foolish desire and a self-mutilating trick ('He will cut off his thumb to please a select crowd'). Prynne's appended 'his part of the soul' may compress Ibn 'Arabi's commentary, where the dove is the holy influence whose 'substance only exists through and in me' and death is the soul's severance from 'this dark body'. The borrowing gives the stanza's 'more and more a peaceful universe' a mystical underside: the lament that threatens death is also the soul's own part calling it out of the phenomenal world. It also cuts against the poem's title, because the gnostic gloss turns a plain example into an allegory.

    quotation. kbgrep "dove's lamentation", 'Tarjuman': 0 hits; 'Arabi': only unrelated hits. Web search 'Prynne "dove's lamentation" Ibn Arabi': nothing. Corroboration: Prynne's 1967 reading list on light-metaphysics sent to Needham (21 Nov 1967) includes Asín Palacios on 'Abenarabi' (Ibn 'Arabi).

    Verified: inside.py 'death hovers because of' and 'the dove's lamentation' (before 1971): every hit is Nicholson's Tarjuman (8 scans) or Landau 1959 quoting it. Read Ode XVI and its commentary in the full djvu text (tarjumanalashwaq00ibnaiala). The Tarjuman was searched for other words of the poem ('racked', 'foolish', 'listless', 'fountain', 'sister' etc.) without further matches.

  127. 'the great pyrotechnist
    who did it all, red from head to foot'     Anthony Trollope, Phineas Redux Brass (1971) · A New Tax on the Counter-Earth · l.6008 · p.172 · new/high

    1874; any edition (e.g. OUP World's Classics); ch. XXXIV, 'The Universe' source ↗

    There would be a blaze and a confusion, in which timid men would doubt whether the constitution would be burned to tinder or only illuminated; but that blaze and that confusion would be dear to Mr. Daubeny if he could stand as the centre figure,--the great pyrotechnist who did it all, red from head to foot with the glare of the squibs with which his own hands were filling all the spaces.

    Daubeny is Trollope's Disraeli. He is the Conservative leader who expects a radical gamble to keep him in office, while the clubs wonder whether the constitution will be 'burned to tinder or only illuminated'. Prynne's draft was sent to Dorn on 1 July 1970, two weeks after Heath's election, with a Spectator cutting by Robert Blake (Disraeli's biographer) on Tory statecraft from Peel and Disraeli. So the 'pyrotechnist' is the Tory showman whose display of 'crisis' (Lord Cromer's warnings) induces 'disbelief stronger even than remedies'. Prynne cuts the quotation before 'with the glare of the squibs', so the redness is left free to mean blush, blood or fire.

    quotation. kbgrep 'pyrotechnist': quoted without a source by Clark (2003). Latter (2014) calls it a quotation that 'remains resistant' to synthesis. kbgrep 'Phineas': no hits. Web search: nothing. Keery (2002) names Trollope's The Prime Minister, not Phineas Redux, for this poem.

    Verified: PG candidate. Gutenberg #18640 read in context. inside.py 'pyrotechnist who did it all' finds only Phineas Redux printings (and its Harper's serialisation) before Prynne.

  128. the limbic mid-brain system W. W. Meissner, S.J., Dreaming as Process Brass (1971) · A New Tax on the Counter-Earth · l.6022 · p.172 · new/low

    International Journal of Psycho-Analysis 49 (1968): 63-79; pp. 64, 70-71 ('the limbic midbrain system', after Nauta 1958) source ↗

    On its own the phrase is a neuroanatomical term. Its value is as corroboration: it occurs in both Meissner papers that the poem quotes. In Meissner's model the limbic-midbrain circuit is the primitive drive centre activated in REM sleep, so 'cash so distraught that the limbic mid-brain system has absorbed its reflex massage' puts money into the dreaming brain stem. 'Limbic midbrain system' is Nauta's standard term, so this is corroboration of the Meissner source only.

    echo. kbgrep 'Meissner': no hits.

    Verified: Full djvu text of IJPA vol. 49 downloaded and grepped. Meissner's companion paper (source of two verbatim quotations below) also has 'limbic midbrain system' (p. 700). The term is Nauta's technical term.

  129. "the transit from drive organization
    to cognitive process."     W. W. Meissner, S.J., Notes on Dreaming: Dreaming as a Cognitive Process Brass (1971) · A New Tax on the Counter-Earth · l.6039 · p.173 · new/high

    International Journal of Psycho-Analysis 49 (1968): 699-708; p. 701 source ↗

    These latter functions are involved in specifically cognitive activities. The transit from drive organization to cognitive process is accomplished in terms of the functions of activated circuits, which are intrinsically cognitional.

    Meissner's paper explains how drive activation in REM sleep becomes the cognitive work of a wish. Prynne uses the sentence for the 'grand stability of dream', in which the truth 'became optional'. The political dream of the Heath election is therefore described literally in the neurophysiology of wish fulfilment. Drive becomes thought by an automatic circuit and not by argument.

  130. The distance of being so reopens
    the millennial landscape, "that we need not even
    think of it as possible."     Anthony Trollope, The Prime Minister Brass (1971) · A New Tax on the Counter-Earth · l.6047 · p.173 · partial/high

    1876; any edition; ch. LXVIII, 'The Prime Minister's Political Creed' source ↗

    "I did not use the word, which is open to many objections. In the first place the millennium, which I have perhaps rashly named, is so distant that we need not even think of it as possible. Men's intellects are at present so various that we cannot even realise the idea of equality ..."

    The Duke of Omnium is explaining the Liberal creed to Phineas: a 'millennium' of equality, a lessening of distances between the coachman and the duke, so distant that one 'need not even think of it as possible'. Prynne's 'distance' and 'millennial landscape' repeat the Duke's argument. Equality postponed indefinitely is the political content of the post-election dream, in which 'being right is not so absolute as being so'. (The same chapter's 'Equality is a dream' may lie behind 'the dream prevails' at l. 6005, though the poem's dream vocabulary is mainly Meissner's.)

    quotation. Keery (Jacket 20, 2002) says that The Prime Minister 'supplies several tropes and a direct quotation' to this poem, but the corpus text does not say which. Clark (2003) quotes the line without a source. Clara Claiborne Park quotes Trollope's sentence independently.

    Verified: inside.py 'need not even think of it as possible' gives Trollope's The Prime Minister as the only pre-1971 source. Gutenberg #2158 read in context.

  131. "the perceptual events of the dream
    produce a partial or temporary reduction in the
    state of need current in the organism."     W. W. Meissner, S.J. (paraphrasing G. S. Klein 1967), Notes on Dreaming: Dreaming as a Cognitive Process Brass (1971) · A New Tax on the Counter-Earth · l.6050 · p.173 · new/high

    International Journal of Psycho-Analysis 49 (1968): 699-708; p. 701 source ↗

    The dream not only reflects the operation of drive mechanisms but, as Klein (1967) suggests, the perceptual events of the dream produce a partial or temporary reduction in the state of need current in the organism. He cites some suggestive evidence to the effect that the intrusion of thirst-satisfying content into the dreams of thirsty subjects was related to a reduction in water consumption after awakening (Bokert, 1965).

    Meissner's evidence is that thirsty sleepers who dream of drinking drink less on waking. So the dream does not only represent need, it partly satisfies it. Prynne makes this the poem's political charge: the dream of the 'great landscape' and of cash 'as a principle of nature' really does reduce need, 'cheap at the price'. It induces a self-made 'gratitude' and 'moment of joy'.

    quotation. kbgrep 'state of need current': only Clark (2003) quoting the poem.

    Verified: Same IJPA scan, read in context, a few lines after the previous quotation. The wording is Meissner's own paraphrase of Klein, not in quotation marks, so Prynne took it from Meissner.

  136. who have therefore no weight or load upon
    their Faculties, nothing to dead or slacken
    the Spring of their Nature, no Concupiscence
    to darken their Understandings, or to pervert
    their Wills, no Indisposition, Languor or
    Weariness occasioned through crazy and
    sickly Vehicles
    ... but are always Fresh,
    Vigorous and Bright, like the life and
    quickness of the Morning, and rejoyce like
    the Sun to run their Course     John Norris (of Bemerton), A Discourse concerning the Doing God's Will on Earth, as it is in Heaven (Matt. vi. 10), in Practical Discourses upon Several Divine Subjects, vol. II Brass (1971) · Of Sanguine Fire · l.6160 · p.177 · partial/high

    1693; repr. 1707 (with the Beatitudes), 1716, 1728; 1716 ed., vol. II, pp. 228-9 source ↗

    BUT now the Holy Angels have none of these impediments; they have either no Bodies, or such as no way incommode or retard, but rather help and further their Faculties ... or if they have Bodies, they are of so refined and clarified a Mould, so nigh to an Immaterial Substance, that Spirit might serve as a common word for both. They have therefore no weight or load upon their Faculties, nothing to dead or slacken the Spring of their Nature, no Concupiscence to darken their Understandings, or to pervert their Wills; no Indisposition, Languor or Weariness occasioned through crazy and sickly Vehicles, but are always Fresh, Vigorous and Bright, like the life and quickness of the Morning, and rejoyce like the Sun to run their Course. They have no Necessities to relieve or provide for ...

    Norris is explaining why angels do God's will perfectly and men do not. Angels have no bodies, or 'Vehicles' so refined that 'Spirit' names both body and soul. So nothing slows their faculties: no concupiscence, no fatigue, no 'crazy and sickly Vehicles'. Prynne breaks the sentence twice with Pie's appetite ('a whiff of apple, even short crust', 'pyloric mill racing'). The Platonist angelology therefore stands against bodies made of pastry, pancreas and spinal fluid. The poem's 'angelic substrate', 'angelic evidence' and 'angelic sweat' are measured against Norris's sweatless, weightless angels. The same page says angels act 'as a Stone would tend toward the Center through an unresisting Medium', which links to the Aristotelian 'natural place' of another Brass title.

    quotation. Keery (Jacket 20, 2002) says Forrest-Thomson does not name the source of 'the italicised description of angelic essences' and does not find it himself. He glosses only the Psalm 19 echo ('rejoyce like the Sun'). Sankar (Cornell PhD, 2012) lists 'Norris, John. Practical Discourse upon the Beatitudes. London: Manship, 1707' in her bibliography, but the corpus OCR shows no in-text identification. kbgrep 'John Norris', 'Bemerton', 'sickly Vehicles': nothing else. Sankar (2012) lists Norris's Practical Discourse upon the Beatitudes in her bibliography, so she probably identified the passage.

Brockwell (1783) and Stackhouse (1743) paraphrase him. Full 1716 djvu text read in context. Prynne keeps Norris's capitals and the spelling 'rejoyce'. His 'who have' replaces Norris's 'They have'. He breaks the sentence at 'Vehicles' and resumes it at 'but are always'.

  142. Aus der Welt
    werden wir nicht fallen, not dashing a foot
    you say, we are so much before and after
    and thus are saved, are safe, are rife.     Michael Balint (quoting Freud quoting C. D. Grabbe, Hannibal), Friendly Expanses—Horrid Empty Spaces 10 Uncollected Poems (1972) · The King of Spain · l.6439 · p.188 · new/high

    International Journal of Psycho-Analysis 36, parts 4–5 (1955), pp. 225–41 (material reworked in Balint, Thrills and Regressions, Hogarth, 1959); the line's famous carrier is Freud, Civilization and its Discontents, ch. 1 n. 1 (Riviere 1930; Strachey 1961); Balint's essay is the specific source the surrounding lines point to; sect. II, p. 231 and n. 8 source ↗

    'If I have understood my friend aright he means the same thing as that consolation offered by an original and somewhat unconventional writer to his hero, contemplating suicide: "Out of this world we cannot fall." So it is a feeling of indissoluble connexion, of belonging inseparably to the external world as a whole.' ... n. 8: Christian Grabbe: Hannibal: 'Ja, aus der Welt werden wir nicht fallen. Wir sind einmal darin.'

    Grabbe's Hannibal says it to console himself before taking poison; Freud uses it to define, ironically, Rolland's 'oceanic' feeling; Balint uses Freud to found his theory of the philobat, who believes the 'friendly expanses' will hold him like the mother or the amniotic sea. Prynne's poem stages exactly this: 'fly down', 'flight deck', 'outrunning the fall', 'are saved, are safe'. The quotation is the poem's thesis of a world one cannot fall out of, given as reassurance whose source is a suicide's consolation. 'Not dashing a foot' (Ps. 91:12 / Matt. 4:6, the temptation to cast oneself down and be caught by angels) doubles the same fantasy of being held while falling.

    quotation. kbgrep 'Aus der Welt', 'nicht fallen', 'Grabbe' (only false hits on 'grabbed'), 'Hannibal', 'Balint': no Prynne-critical source. WebSearch 'Prynne' + 'King of Spain' + Balint/Grabbe: nothing.

    Verified: Read the full djvu text of IJP 36 parts 4–5 (archive.org). The Grabbe line is also in Freud, Das Unbehagen in der Kultur (1930) ch. 1 n. 1 and in the Riviere and Strachey translations (inside.py, 96 hits, all Freud and Freud-derived). Balint is preferred over Freud because the same essay supplies 'subdued nondescript humming' four lines later in the poem (see next finding) and the poem's vocabulary of flying, falling, safety and skill.

  143. The
    subdued nondescript humming of the night sky.     Michael Balint, Friendly Expanses—Horrid Empty Spaces (self-quoting Primary Love and Psycho-Analytic Technique, Hogarth, 1952) 10 Uncollected Poems (1972) · The King of Spain · l.6443 · p.188 · new/high

    International Journal of Psycho-Analysis 36, parts 4–5 (1955), pp. 225–41; first in Primary Love and Psycho-Analytic Technique (London: Hogarth, 1952); IJP 36, p. 241 (closing paragraph); Primary Love (1952), scan leaf n298 source ↗

    Sadly enough, we have almost completely neglected to enrich our understanding of these very early, very primitive, phenomena by creating theoretical notions and coining technical terms using the experiences, imagery, and implications of other spheres. Such spheres are, among others, feeling of warmth, rhythmic noises and movements, subdued nondescript humming, the irresistible and overwhelming effects of tastes and smells, of close bodily contact, of tactile and muscle sensations especially in the hands, and the undeniable power of any and all of these for provoking and allaying anxieties and suspicions, blissful contentment and dire and desperate loneliness.

    A three-word string found nowhere else in the archive, and it comes from the same Balint essay as the Grabbe line three lines earlier, which makes the attribution secure. In Balint the humming is one of the pre-verbal sensations of primary love, the undifferentiated harmony with mother and environment. Prynne moves it to 'the night sky', the philobat's 'friendly expanse', so the oceanic infant state becomes a cosmic one. The line therefore names the feeling the poem then puts under strain with deuterium, fusion and 'the fast breeder in top gear'. 'O so skilled is he' later in the poem also matches Balint's dictum 'no philobatism without skill', and 'floating down to the cup' matches his 'floating dreams'.

    quotation. kbgrep 'nondescript' and 'Balint': no relevant hit. WebSearch 'Prynne' 'nondescript humming': nothing.

    Verified: inside.py 'nondescript humming' (no date limit): 3 hits before 1973, all this Balint passage (IJP 1955; Primary Love 1952/53; Rheingold 1964 quoting Balint). olinside.py gives Primary Love scan leaf n298. Read the passage in the IJP djvu text.

  144. And thus the good die first, and they

    Beside yon spring I stood, / And eyed its waters till we seemed to feel / One sadness, they and I. For them a bond / Of brotherhood is broken: time has been / When, every day, the touch of human hand / Dislodged the natural sleep that binds them up / In mortal stillness; and they ministered / To human comfort. Stooping down to drink, / Upon the slimy foot-stone I espied / The useless fragment of a wooden bowl ... I loved her / As my own child. O sir! the good die first, / And they whose hearts are dry as summer dust / Burn to the socket.

    This is the Wanderer's turn from the ruined spring to Margaret's story in the Ruined Cottage section of The Excursion. The good who die first are the ones who loved, and those who survive have hearts dry as dust; under the poem's 'fast breeder in top gear', burning 'to the socket' (a candle used up) also reads as the energy economy.

    quotation. kbgrep 'summer dust', 'burn to the socket', 'good die first': no hit. Prynne's own lecture 'Huts' (Textual Practice 2008) discusses The Ruined Cottage and Margaret's dwelling, so the source is in his range, but the borrowing in this poem is not recorded. A familiar quotation (inside.py 2127 hits), so the source is certain but not obscure.

    Verified: Read in Turner's 1874 edition (archive.org djvu text), ll. 484–502; the Gutenberg match also gives Bartlett's Familiar Quotations and Coleridge (Morley ed.) quoting it. Prynne replaces 'O sir!' with 'And thus' and moves the line break; otherwise verbatim.

That is Balint's ocnophil defending his choice of home, and Balint notes that the safe place in children's games is always called 'house' or 'home'. Prynne gives the question to a cheap imported toy. The heroic choice of the vale becomes a 'made in Hong Kong' trinket, which links the poem's colonial-trade line (nutmeg, 'made in Korea', 'exotic colonial toys') to Wordsworth's domestic retreat. Two Wordsworth lifts ten lines apart confirm that the second is deliberate.

Prynne sets it against the boy's 'triangular sling' (a first-aid term) and the 'torsion song' under glass.   151. Aversion to that, in his jacket, as the
    sun falls, informing water by flake
    and mail. And bringeth to a kingdom:     Wisdom of Solomon (Apocrypha), Authorized (King James) Version Into the Day (1972) · Into the Day · l.6871 · p.207 · new/medium

    AV Apocrypha; Wisdom 6:17-20 source ↗

    For the very true beginning of her is the desire of discipline; and the care of discipline is love; And love is the keeping of her laws; and the giving heed unto her laws is the assurance of incorruption; And incorruption maketh us near unto God: Therefore the desire of wisdom bringeth to a kingdom.

    'And bringeth to a kingdom' is the final link of the sorites in Wisdom 6, where each term leads to the next: desire of discipline, love, keeping of laws, incorruption, nearness to God, and so 'the desire of wisdom bringeth to a kingdom'. Prynne cuts away the subject and opens with its opposite, 'Aversion'. The archaic verb is left hanging after a colon, and the 'kingdom' it reaches turns out 'brown and peaty by conjecture'. The ladder to wisdom ends in bog. The confidence is medium because the borrowed string is short. But the 'eth' form, the initial 'And' of a chained verse, and the nearby 'elated by counsel' all point to the sapiential text.

    quotation. kbgrep 'bringeth to a kingdom', 'desire of wisdom', 'Wisdom of Solomon': 0 hits.

  152. the sky
    in chance halo, cadentia
    sydera caelo.     Virgil, Aeneid Into the Day (1972) · Into the Day · l.6881 · p.207 · new/high

    any Latin text (e.g. J. F. C. Richards, Virgil: Aeneid I, II, IV, VI, 1960); Aeneid II.8-9 source ↗

    et iam nox umida caelo / praecipitat suadentque cadentia sidera somnos

    Prynne fuses the two halves of Aeneid II.8-9, 'nox umida caelo / praecipitat ... cadentia sidera', into a Latin tag, 'the stars falling from the sky'. In Virgil the setting stars mark the late hour when Aeneas, asked by Dido, starts the story of Troy's last night, so the tag brings in the poem's run from night towards day, and with it the onset of a narrative of ruin. In the early-modern spelling 'sydera' it reads as a learned commonplace, which the next sentence brings down to the punter at the pit. The 'chance halo' points to the other reading of 'cadentia sidera' as shooting stars, false constellations, so this is the poem's sky as accident and not as fixed order. That sets up the Anaximandrian 'fixed order / of time' two lines later.

Richards 1960; Angelitti, Le stelle che cadono, 1898, which discusses whether Virgil's 'cadentia' means setting or shooting stars). The exact form 'cadentia sydera caelo' has only two IA hits: Prynne's Poems (1982) and Peter Bayley, French Pulpit Oratory 1598-1650 (CUP, 1980), where a 17th-century French sermon quotes 'ces fausses constellations que le grand Poete nomme, Cadentia sydera caelo' beside the stick that looks bent in water (searched inside frenchpulpitorat0000bayl).   153. a flower for his sister and all
    their injustice in the fixed order
    of time: by and by. ... fixed injustice gives the orange its
    juice     Anaximander (DK 12 B 1), in the translation used by Harold Cherniss, Aristotle's Criticism of Presocratic Philosophy Into the Day (1972) · Into the Day · l.6885 · p.207 · new/high

    rendering shared by Cherniss (1935/1964), Hugh Miller (1947) and the DSB I (1970); Prynne's copy not fixed; Cherniss 1935, App. (IA scan leaf n446); DSB I (leaf n650) source ↗

    [they] make recompense to one another for their injustice in the fixed order of time (Cherniss); [they] make reparation to one another for their injustice in the fixed order of time (DSB 1970)

    This is the oldest surviving sentence of Greek philosophy: things perish into what they came from 'and make reparation to one another for their injustice in the fixed order of time'. Prynne keeps 'injustice' and 'fixed order of time' and then turns the phrase over into 'fixed injustice gives the orange its juice'. Cosmic retribution becomes the pressing of fruit, and the 'by and by' of payment deferred. The source corrects Nolan's Shakespearean reading. The 'fixed order' is not a social hierarchy but the cosmic law of coming into being and passing away, a fitting text for a book about the sun's daily course. The punter at the pit and the 'flower for his sister' are fitted into an Anaximandrian economy of debt and repayment.

    quotation. kbgrep 'fixed order of time': 0 hits. Nolan ('Capital Calves') reads 'fixed injustice' as Shakespeare's Ulyssean 'degree' and does not see Anaximander. The kb hits for 'Anaximander' (Nolan, Sutherland) concern other matters.

    Verified: inside.py 'injustice in the fixed order of time': 14 hits, all renderings of the Anaximander fragment (Cherniss 1935/1964; Miller 1947; DSB 1970) plus Prynne himself. Other translations differ: Burnet has 'according to the ordering of time', and Robinson 1968 has 'according to the ordinance'. So this specific rendering of κατὰ τὴν τοῦ χρόνου τάξιν is the one Prynne uses.

  154. A line of zero interval
    fits between the pair of points and
    past them.     D. W. Sciama, Modern Cosmology Into the Day (1972) · Into the Day · l.6912 · p.209 · new/high

    Cambridge University Press, 1971; ch. on light propagation in Robertson-Walker models (IA scan leaf n246) source ↗

    the path of a light ray through space-time is given in relativity by a line of zero interval between any pair of points along it, that is, by putting ds = 0 in the Robertson-Walker [metric]

    Sciama, Hawking's supervisor at Cambridge, defines a light ray as a null line, a line of zero interval 'between any pair of points along it'. Prynne keeps the definition but pushes it 'past them', so a line of zero length between two points also runs beyond them. That is the paradox of the null geodesic: light has no proper time. The next image is the bird 'looping and calling' and 'desire on a single button' held in a 'prolonged intake of breath'. So the lyric moment, a breath held between two points, is made the same as the timelessness of light.

  155. at the lumen, "as the light
    of a great number of candles." ... One flame
    behind the other, in this line
    we are invaded.     John Michell, On the Means of Discovering the Distance, Magnitude, &c. of the Fixed Stars, in Consequence of the Diminution of the Velocity of their Light ... Into the Day (1972) · Into the Day · l.6980 · p.212 · new/high

    Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 74 (1784), 35-57; §26, p. 49 source ↗

    This universal and excessive brightness of the whole surface is probably owing to an atmosphere, which being luminous throughout, and in some measure also transparent, the light, proceeding from a considerable depth of it, all arrives at the eye; in the same manner as the light of a great number of candles would do, if they were placed one behind another, and their flames were sufficiently transparent to permit the light of the more distant ones to pass through those that were nearer, without any interruption.

    Michell's 1784 paper is the first to propose 'dark stars', bodies so massive that their own gravity would hold back their light. That is the 18th-century origin of the black-hole physics that runs through the rest of the poem (see the Zel'dovich & Novikov finding). The quoted simile is Michell's model of the sun's luminous atmosphere: light from many transparent flames, one behind another, all reaching the eye. Prynne turns this into a figure of lovers or travellers lined up 'in this line' and 'invaded' by one another's light. The poem then moves to 'Occulted by the great disk ... scant light now', which reverses the image: light is cut off instead of let through. So the quotation is both scientific history and the poem's main figure, mutual transparency, which collapse later swallows.

    quotation. kbgrep 'great number of candles': 0 hits. The only kb hits for 'Michell' are John Michell the 1960s ley-line writer. The web finds nothing linking Prynne to this paper.

    Verified: inside.py: the exact phrase has 22 IA hits, every one a copy of Michell's 1784 paper or its 1785 reprint in the London Magazine. Read in the paper's djvu text (paper-doi-10_1098_rstl_1784_0008), §26, p. 49. Prynne's 'One flame behind the other' renders Michell's next clause, 'placed one behind another, and their flames'.

  156. spacelike
    in two regions and timelike in
    the two others     Ya. B. Zel'dovich and I. D. Novikov, Relativistic Astrophysics, Volume 1: Stars and Relativity Into the Day (1972) · Into the Day · l.6982 · p.212 · partial/medium

    University of Chicago Press, 1971; §3.12 'The R- and T-Regions of Schwarzschild Spacetime', pp. 110-15 (and the definition repeated at IA leaf n554) source ↗

    If ∇A is spacelike, the given event is in an R-region. If ∇A is timelike, the event is in a T-region. If ∇A is lightlike, the event is in neither an R-region nor a T-region. ... The locations of the R- and T-regions in R* and r* coordinates are shown ... However, as demonstrated by Kruskal (1960), this system is also incomplete

    Novikov's R- and T-regions divide the extended Schwarzschild spacetime by whether the gradient of the radius is spacelike or timelike. In the Kruskal diagram that gives two regions of each kind: the two exteriors, where one can stand still, and the black-hole and white-hole interiors, where 'r' becomes a time and motion must go one way. Prynne's 'spacelike / in two regions and timelike in / the two others' is a compressed caption of that four-quadrant map. 'We cross / into the ship hardily' is then the crossing of a horizon into a T-region, where, in the book's sense, 'no fate from the orbit comes / ashore with us'. Read with the 'region inside the sphere' passage two pages later, it shows that the poem's travellers follow the world lines of the book. Extends the Zel'dovich & Novikov entry at l. 7026.

    allusion. Zel'dovich & Novikov is cited by Katko (Glossator 2, 2010) for The Plant Time Manifold Transcripts, and this project's first pass found it for Into the Day ll. 7026ff. The R/T-region borrowing at l. 6982 is not recorded (the first pass left it in 'unverified' with no source text). kbgrep 'T-region': no hits.

  157. The nervous one sings
    in the mountains, hoar cycloid above
    his brow, his feet numb, "the bugle
    ringing through a vast pine wood
    to keep us together."     Thomas Hood, Letter to [Charles] Wright, on accompanying a Prussian regiment on the march (Coblenz, 1835) Into the Day (1972) · Into the Day · l.7004 · p.212 · new/high

    Memorials of Thomas Hood, ed. by his daughter [F. F. Broderip] (London: Moxon, 1860), vol. 1; reprinted in Walter Jerrold, Thomas Hood: His Life and Times (1907; repr. 1968, 1969); Memorials vol. 1, p. 229 source ↗

    I assure you sometimes I have almost asked myself the question, whether I was I, seeming to be so much out of my ordinary life,—for example, on horseback, following, or rather belonging to, a company of soldiers; the bugle ringing through a vast pine wood to keep us together, or the men perhaps singing Polish songs in chorus, for this is a Polish regiment chiefly.

    Prynne quotes Hood's account of riding with a Prussian (largely Polish) regiment through Germany. Hood had been 'taken very ill in the night' just before the march, and he wonders 'whether I was I'. That fits 'The nervous one ... his feet numb', and Hood's 'men ... singing Polish songs' becomes 'sings in the mountains'. The comic, invalid English poet lost in a German forest sits beside the apostrophe to Mörike two lines earlier, the Swabian poet of nervous retreat. In the poem, the bugle 'to keep us together' is a signal across a field that holds a moving company together. Prynne at once recodes this as physics: 'In this local / inertial frame'. The company on the march becomes a comoving frame, held together by a signal.

  158. Here begins the world line of the sphere. ... The region inside the sphere
    is shaded. ... This is
    another flame, not ours ... The shell
    crossing is sport ... we pass layer after layer     Ya. B. Zel'dovich and I. D. Novikov, Relativistic Astrophysics, Volume 1: Stars and Relativity Into the Day (1972) · Into the Day · l.7026 · p.213 · new/high

    trans. Eli Arlock, ed. Kip S. Thorne and W. David Arnett (University of Chicago Press, 1971); §4.5-4.6 ('Through the Event Horizon'), pp. 145-46, Fig. 26 source ↗

    particles from the interior of the sphere may drift out across the sphere's surface ('shell crossing') ... If adjacent layers of matter do not pass through each other, the density does not reach infinity anywhere ... Figure 26 shows the spacetime for this solution, which is similar to Kruskal spacetime, as well as the world line of a particle on the sphere's boundary (ABCD). The region inside the sphere is shaded. ... This region ... is not the same as the region in which the contraction originated, but is a different one ... it is actually 'another' [universe]

    The second half of Into the Day is partly a caption to Zel'dovich & Novikov's Figure 26. A charged sphere collapses through its event horizon and bounces instead of reaching a singularity, then re-expands into a region 'not the same as the region in which the contraction originated'. Prynne's 'Here begins the world line of the sphere', 'The region inside the sphere / is shaded', 'The shell / crossing is sport' and 'we pass layer after layer' come straight from that page. 'The travellers come to the gate' and 'This is / another flame, not ours' read as the passage through the wormhole into 'another' universe, which Prynne's letter of October 1971 already joked about. The child, the bird and the ship of the lyric are mapped onto a Penrose-Kruskal diagram. The book's diurnal course 'into the day' is thus also a passage through a horizon that cannot be reversed, which is why it ends 'to darker fields we go'. 'spacelike / in two regions and timelike in / the two others' (l. 6984) also fits the Kruskal diagram.

    quotation. kbgrep 'Zeldovich', 'shell crossing', 'inside the sphere is shaded': 0 hits. Stone-Richards quotes 'Here begins the world line of the sphere' and 'shear at the flowline' as examples of line imagery but gives no source. Katko ('Relativistic Phytosophy') cites Z&N vol. II (1975/1983) for the much later 'Plant Time Manifold Transcripts'. Its use in Into the Day is not recorded.

    Verified: inside.py 'region inside the sphere is shaded' (pre-1973): 2 hits, both this book. Read in the djvu text of the full IA copy: the sentence, 'shell crossing', 'adjacent layers' and 'the world line of a particle on the sphere's boundary' all fall within one page of the charged-sphere collapse passage. Prynne's letter to Dorn of 24 Oct 1971 cites 'Zeldovich & Novikov 1971, p. 169' and Hawking on matter falling through a 'wormhole' to 'emerge into another universe'.

  159. After feints the heart steadies,
    pointwise invariant, by the drown'd
    light of her fire. In the set course
    we pass layer after layer, loving
    what we still know.     Boethius, trans. 'I.T.' (1609), The Consolation of Philosophy Into the Day (1972) · Into the Day · l.7056 · p.214 · new/high

    I.T. translation (1609), as printed with modern spelling in the Loeb Boethius, ed. H. F. Stewart and E. K. Rand (1918; repr. 1953, 1962). The original spelling 'drown'd' survives in the 1609 text and in its reprints (e.g. the 1963 edition on IA; Lathrop, Translations from the Classics, 1967); Book V, metre 3 source ↗

    But our dull soul, covered with members blind, / Knows not the secret laws which things do bind, / By the drown'd light of her oppressed fire. / Why then, the hidden notes of things to find, / Doth she with such a love of truth desire? / If she knows that which she doth so require, / Why wisheth she known things to know again?

    This metre states Boethius's problem of foreknowledge against freedom. The soul, blinded by the body, sees truth only by the 'drown'd light' of its own oppressed fire. Yet it longs to know again what it already knows, which is the Platonic doctrine of recollection. I.T. already has 'her oppressed fire', where 'her' is the soul; Prynne keeps the pronoun and drops 'oppressed', and any shift to the beloved comes from the poem's context. His 'loving / what we still know' compresses Boethius's question, 'Doth she with such a love of truth desire ... known things to know again?' Set in the relativistic close of the book ('pointwise invariant', 'Timelike delirium'), the borrowing frames the ending as recollection through a horizon: the daughter 'willed back' is what the soul half remembers.

    adaptation. kbgrep "drown'd light", 'oppressed fire': 0 hits. Boethius is not linked to this poem in the corpus or on the web.

    Verified: inside.py "by the drown'd light" (pre-1973): 3 hits, all I.T.'s Boethius (1963 ed.; Lathrop 1967). Read in full in the Loeb (1918) djvu text, Book V metre 3. The Loeb prints 'drowned'; Prynne's elided 'drown'd' follows the original spelling.

  162. So the tenant comes back under his arch
    of blood, affirming its pulse ... The force for existence
    composes a colony of black spots ... This is a passion which throws over
    the hostage to violent ocular convulsion.     Benedict de Spinoza, The Ethics, Part III, 'General Definition of the Emotions' Wound Response (1974) · Pigment Depot · l.7255 · p.221 · new/high

    trans. R. H. M. Elwes, Chief Works of Spinoza (Bohn, 1883; Dover reprint 1951); Project Gutenberg #3800; Ethics III, end: General Definition of the Emotions and Explanation source ↗

    Emotion, which is called a passivity of the soul, is a confused idea, whereby the mind affirms concerning its body, or any part thereof, a force for existence (existendi vis) greater or less than before, and by the presence of which the mind is determined to think of one thing rather than another. ... its power of action or force for existence is increased or diminished, helped or hindered.

    Spinoza's definition supplies three terms in Prynne's opening sequence: the mind 'affirms' concerning its body; what it affirms is a 'force for existence'; and the whole state is a 'passion' (the weakest link, a common word). Prynne gives the affirming to the body's 'tenant' and its pulse. The force for existence does not grow or shrink here. It 'composes a colony of black spots' (pigment, or melanoma), and the 'passion' becomes an ocular convulsion. The borrowing sets Spinoza's account of emotion as a confused idea of the body's changing power against a clinical scene of pigment, drugs and convulsion. The tenant who 'does not command the freehold' is the mind that does not own its body.

  167. Is the throat
    dry, no it is mine and lined with marrow;
    bone on the other hand "can be here today
    and gone tomorrow."     E. N. Willmer, Cytology and Evolution Wound Response (1974) · Landing Area · l.7350 · p.224 · new/high

    2nd edn, New York and London: Academic Press, 1970; chapter on the skeletal tissues (osteoblasts, dentine and bone); IA leaf n674 source ↗

    Dentine tends to stay where it is put, though in some animals it is capable of being continuously augmented; bone, on the other hand, can be here today and gone tomorrow. It is always in a state of flux, adjusting its position and shape, in some ill-understood manner, to the mechanical stresses of the moment.

    Prynne's quotation marks surround a cliché, and the source shows that the cliché is a precise histological statement: bone, unlike dentine, is always being resorbed and laid down again. Prynne also takes Willmer's 'on the other hand', so the stable term that Willmer sets against bone (dentine, a tissue of the teeth) becomes the speaker's dry throat, 'mine and lined with marrow'. The proverb of fickleness is literalised as remodelling. In a sequence about wounds, blood counts and 'some kind of bone infection', the body's own frame is shown to be a state of flux, a bone that can be gone tomorrow. Prynne's quotation marks open exactly at 'can be', where Willmer's words continue after 'bone, on the other hand,', so the unquoted lead-in is Willmer's too; Willmer was Professor of Histology at Cambridge.

    quotation. kbgrep 'here today' finds only unrelated hits; kbgrep 'Willmer' finds nothing. No critic in the corpus names Willmer or traces this quotation.

    Verified: The idiom alone has 10,000+ IA hits, so I ran Boolean searches that joined it to bone-physiology terms ('here today and gone tomorrow" AND "osteoclasts'). Two physiology books came back. I then searched inside both. Willmer has the whole run 'bone, on the other hand, can be here today and gone tomorrow' (inside.py in-item, both IA scans cytologyevolutio0000will and _t6b1; olinside.py gives leaf n674). I rebuilt the sentence before and after it from overlapping in-item snippets ('Dentine tends to stay where it is put, though', 'being continuously augmented', 'state of flux, adjusting its position and shape', 'mechanical stresses of the moment'). Gould, Treatise on Collagen II (1968), uses the idiom of collagen ('sign of life can literally be "here today and gone tomorrow"'), but it does not have 'bone, on the other hand'. The printed page number was not recovered (the book is lending-only). I did not check whether the 1960 first edition has the sentence.

  171. the white bees
    swarm out from the open voice gap     Hans Christian Andersen, The Snow Queen, in Fairy Tales of Hans Christian Andersen Wound Response (1974) · Again in the Black Cloud · l.7505 · p.230 · new/high

    trans. Mrs H. B. Paull (London: Warne, 1867 and many reprints); Project Gutenberg #27200; 'The Snow Queen', Second and Seventh Stories source ↗

    "See there are the white bees swarming," said Kay's old grandmother one day when it was snowing. "Have they a queen bee?" asked the little boy (Paull). Boner: "It is the white bees that are swarming," said Kay's old grandmother.

    In The Snow Queen the 'white bees' are snowflakes. Their queen is the Snow Queen, and a splinter of the devil's mirror lodges in Kay's eye and heart while they swarm. Prynne's bees 'swarm out from the open voice gap', so the snowstorm comes out of the mouth. This fits the poem's shouts and its later 'snow-fields'. The source turns the poem's scene of injury into the fairy tale's: a child wounded by a speck of glass, cut off from love and recall ('Who can see what he loves, / again or before, as the injury shears / past the curve of recall'). Andersen's mirror is shattered into 'a hundred million and more pieces' and his frozen lake is 'broken on its surface into a thousand forms'. Prynne's 'the hour / is crazed by fracture' and 'half-silvered' keep the language of mirror glass. Henry Van Dyke's 'The White Bees' (1909) is the main other English use of the kenning, but it has no children or mirror, so Andersen remains likelier.

WebSearch 'Prynne' 'Again in the Black Cloud' 'Snow Queen': nothing. Letters store: no Andersen mention.

The earliest English ones are Andersen (The Will-o'-the-Wisps are in Town, 1867: 'the white bees swarm, and sting the face') and Andersen derivatives. 'White bees' is the Danish folk kenning for snowflakes, and Andersen made it current in English.

    In Dunsany a boy waits at dusk on an Irish bog for the wild geese to come in. The sky is spent as a source of light but still holds the light, and the birds show against it. In the Oracle the bees are the Ideas, the noetic thoughts of the Father, which swarm through the cosmic wombs. In the PTM they are also the been/bean/bee of the Bean News pun.   196. itself after the recognition of polynucleotides streaming out from the epoch such as shyne in our speech like the glorious stars in Firmament. There is a set of loops somewhere in this great & forcible floud like the aurora Henry Peacham (the elder), The Garden of Eloquence, Conteyning the Figures of Grammer and Rhetorick The Plant Time Manifold Transcripts (1974) · The Plant Time Manifold Transcripts · l.7929 · p.242 · new/high

    London: H. Jackson, 1577 (STC 19497); facsimile, English Linguistics 1500-1800 no. 267, Menston: Scolar Press, 1971; Epistle dedicatory to John Aylmer, Bishop of London, sigs. A.ii-A.iii source ↗

    to set therein such Fyguratyue Flowers both of Grammer and Rhetorick, as doe yeelde the sweete sauour of Eloquence, & present to the eyes the goodly and bewtiful coulors of Eloquution: such as shyne in our speech like the glorious stars in Firmament: suche as bewtify it as flowers ... For by Fygures, as it were by [conduits?], the great & forcible floud of Eloquence, is most plentifully ... powred forth

    Both the old spellings ('shyne', 'floud', '&') and the capital 'Firmament' are those of the 1577 first edition. The 1593 revision rewrote this epistle, so Prynne used the 1577 text, probably in the 1971 Scolar facsimile. In Peacham the things that 'shyne in our speech like the glorious stars' are rhetorical figures, or 'Flowers'. The 'negative flower of the Cosmos' at the end of the Transcripts is therefore also a flower of rhetoric, and the 'set of loops' is a set of figures (tropes, 'turns'). The 'great & forcible floud' is Peacham's flood of Eloquence, which the PTM sets next to the polynucleotide stream of the genetic code. So the genetic text and the rhetorical text become one 'speech' at the close. Intermediaries do not explain both clauses: Baldwin (1944/1956) quotes 'shyne in our speech ... Firmament' without the 'forcible floud', and Plett (1975) only the 'floud'; only Peacham 1577 (or its 1971 facsimile) has both.

  199. And a wound is not
    anything lost     David Daube, Studies in Biblical Law High Pink on Chrome (1975) · High Pink on Chrome: 'The halter of melon seeds, dyed in' · l.8052 · p.250 · new/high

    Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1947; ch. III, 'Lex Talionis', c. pp. 104-5 source ↗

    You can replace a life or organ lost, but you cannot properly speak of replacing a wound. A wound is not anything lost, but a damage inflicted, and you do not put anything 'in the place of' a damage. Yet in Exodus we find enjoined 'burning for burning, wound for wound, stripe for stripe'.

    Daube's sentence is the hinge of his argument that the talion formula is about restitution, not revenge. A life or an eye can be 'given in the place of' what was lost, but a wound is a damage inflicted, so the formula's last clause 'burning for burning, wound for wound' fails as compensation. Prynne quotes the first half of the sentence and, six lines later, the Exodus clause that Daube's very next sentence introduces. The stanza moves from flattery and silence (Sanderson) to the legal problem of what a wound costs and who can repay it. The shortened 'innermost and motionless boundary, burning for burning' then sets Aristotle's place beside a retaliation that cannot restore anything. Daube's 'cut' and Job's 'touch his bone' give the stanza's opening question, 'What then will cut to his bone', its context. Cross-reference the Aristotle and Exodus 21:25 entries at ll. 8057-8058: Daube's next sentence introduces the Exodus clause.

    quotation. kbgrep 'Daube' and 'anything lost': no Daube in the corpus. Ryan Dobran ('How Does a Wound Respond?', draft essay, 2021) quotes 'a wound is not | anything lost' and reads it through the biology of wound hormones. He does not name a source. The first pass recorded only the Exodus 21:25 'burning for burning' (line 8058).

    Verified: inside.py 'a wound is not anything lost' gave 5 hits with no year: two IA scans of Daube (1947), Prynne's Poems (1982), and nothing else. A search inside the Daube item (studiesinbiblica0000davi_s2w4) gave the surrounding sentences: 'organ lost', 'replacing a wound', 'damage inflicted, and you do not put anything ‘in the place of’ a damage. Yet in Exodus we find enjoined ‘burning ...'. The chapter heading 'Lex Talionis' and running heads for pp. 104 and 105 appear in the nearby snippets. The same chapter also discusses 'B’s cut to be in the place of A’s cut' and quotes Job 2:5, 'touch his bone and flesh'. Compare the stanza's first line, 'What then will cut to his bone'.

  201. The innermost and
    motionless boundary, burning for burning,
    we dash outwards through the smoke.     Aristotle, trans. R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye, Physica High Pink on Chrome (1975) · High Pink on Chrome: 'What then will cut to his bone, when silence' · l.8057 · p.250 · partial/high

    Hence we conclude that the innermost motionless boundary of what contains is place.

    In Aristotle, place is the inner surface of the container, which keeps a thing where it is. Prynne joins this definition to the lex talionis ('burning for burning', Exod. 21:25), and the 'we' then 'dash outwards through the smoke', like Aristotelian fire moving up to its natural place. Since it follows 'a wound is not / anything lost', the Exodus formula ('burning for burning, wound for wound') is clearly in view. The containing boundary of the body (skin, the 'flushed ledges') is the place where retaliation and treatment take effect. This is one of three verbatim lifts from the same translation of the Physics in poems 6-9 (see lines 8067 and 8105). The phrase is widely quoted in secondary literature (Edel 1934, Evans 1964, Bochner 1966), so the two other Physics lifts fix the Hardie-Gaye translation.

All these things pass to and fro in the world from one hand to another, and so to another, and another, ever and anon, upon some casualty or other, many times in a moment; shifting masters; and seldom stay long in a place.

    Sanderson, glossing Horace (Satires II.2), preaches contentment: property is never really ours, but passes 'from one hand to another'. Prynne breaks off the sentence and adds 'belayed', a word for making a rope fast, so that the circulation is stopped. The same poem ends 'in high-level, foisted arbitrage'. The sermon's view of worldly goods as transient becomes the image of commodity and capital flow, which the poem's 'storm / of a sexual fury' and 'antigens' tie to the food trade in contaminated grain. The theme of contentment may also be heard in the next poem's close, 'where / the journal rests and is content'. Sanderson goes on, 'When one would think we had them fast, either they take them wings ... and fly away', which supports reading 'belayed' (made fast) as Prynne's reply.

    quotation. kbgrep 'to and fro in the world', 'Sanderson': no relevant hits. Eltringham (2018) quotes these lines without a source.

    Verified: inside.py 'pass to and fro in the world' gave 19 hits before 1976, nearly all Sanderson's sermons (1656, 1671, 1673, 1681, 1686, Works 1854). I read the passage in the vol. 1 djvu text (running head 'PHIL. IV. 11. Serm. i. AD AULAM. 133'). This candidate was also in the PG 4-gram list (line 8109), which gave only generic sources.

  208. So dream after dream ensues, William Cowper, The Task High Pink on Chrome (1975) · High Pink on Chrome: 'Heavy metal then is the storm' · l.8112 · p.252 · new/high

    1785; any standard ed., e.g. Poetical Works, ed. H. S. Milford (Oxford, 1934); Book III, "The Garden", c. ll. 127-29 source ↗

    ... pursuing fancied happiness, still wooed / And never won. Dream after dream ensues; / And still they dream that they shall still succeed, / And still are disappointed.

    Cowper's line is about the worldly who chase 'fancied happiness' and are always disappointed. It comes from Book III, 'The Garden', the Georgic part of The Task, in which the retired gardener sets the cultivated plot against the busy world. That is the right model for High Pink's chemically compromised pastoral. Prynne follows it at once with a half-line of Pound (see line 8113)., and the two then run into 'organic dust & its antigens'.

    quotation. Eltringham (2018, p. 11) quotes 'dream after dream / ensues' and reads it as reverie without naming Cowper. kbgrep finds no Cowper attribution.

    Verified: inside.py 'dream after dream ensues' gave 759 hits, mostly Cowper's Task and anthologies of it (Beauties of Cowper, 1801; Milford's Oxford ed.). The hit in Hone's Political House that Jack Built (1819) is itself a quotation of Cowper. I saw the Cowper wording in the IA snippets of the Beauties and the Milford edition.

  209. blind eyes and shadows conspire

    Canzoni (London, 1911); Personae (1926 and later); Pound re-quotes the line in Canto XCI (Rock-Drill, 1955): '"Blind eyes and shadows" / to enter the presence at sunrise', an equally likely proximate source; ll. 1-2 source ↗

    In Pound's poem, the lady's grace is light that dwells among 'blind eyes and shadows that are formed as men' and melts them 'into song'. Prynne keeps the dark half of the line and drops the light. The 'blind eyes and shadows' do not become song; they 'conspire / to organic dust & its antigens', the particulate matter of immune reaction. Prynne's teaching note calls the poem's idiom 'Victorian-romantic daintiness', which helps explain why its Cavalcantian light becomes dust here. The next poem opens 'Get out of this, dainty blood'.

    quotation. kbgrep 'Ballatetta' finds only Prynne's own teaching note on the poem (Caius papers, last modified 2006). No critic links the line to High Pink.

    Verified: inside.py 'blind eyes and shadows that are formed as men' gave 56 hits, all Pound (A Selection of Poems, 1940; Jackson, Early Poetry of Ezra Pound, 1968). Prynne's Caius teaching anthology on Pound ('pound1' in the kb) prints Ballatetta in full with a note.

  210. If I
    had given less, or given more,
    it might have been prudent too.     Henry Hammond, Of Will-Worship (1644) High Pink on Chrome (1975) · High Pink on Chrome: 'What he says they must do is' · l.8145 · p.254 · new/high

    in Severall Tracts (London, 1646), and The Workes of ... Henry Hammond, vol. 1 (London, 1674); also appended to later eds. of A Practicall Catechisme (e.g. 1652); Of Will-Worship, sect. 42 source ↗

    To this I answer, 1. That every man is not bound under pain of sin to be prudent, or pious, or merciful in such a degree; there is a great latitude in prudence, and piety, and in mercifulness, I may give so much, as will denominate me merciful ... nay, I may in prudence give so much to such a man, and yet this not so consist in an indivisible point, but that if I had given less, or given more, it might have been prudent too.

    Hammond is arguing that voluntary alms, which go beyond what is commanded, are not sinful, because prudence has a range and is not a single point. In the poem the casuist's 'given' is lowered onto a scene where, as Eltringham shows, people 'must ... actually starve beforehand' or eat mercury-dressed seed grain. The next line, 'This furtive admission of degrees', glosses Hammond's 'in such a degree': the poem shows a moral calculus of how much to give being carried over into the dose-and-ration arithmetic of famine relief. Poem 21 then lifts the clause just before this one ('a great latitude in prudence'), which shows that the borrowing is deliberate.

    quotation. kbgrep 'prudent too', 'latitude in prudence', 'Hammond', 'Practical Catechism': no relevant hits. Eltringham (2018) and Dobran (2021), the main source studies of High Pink, do not name Hammond.

    Verified: Found by an n-gram match of the whole sequence against the IA djvu text of Hammond's 1674 Workes (running head 'Of Will-worship', marginal 'Sect. 42'). I read the passage in context. inside.py confirms the same sentence in the 1646 Severall Tracts and the 1652 Practicall Catechisme. Prynne's wording is verbatim apart from the line breaks.

  211. How do
    they get in if not by straying, where growth
    is a kind of success across the open window.     Samuel Butler, Luck, or Cunning, as the Main Means of Organic Modification? High Pink on Chrome (1975) · High Pink on Chrome: 'In the lane the overdrive is shot sideways' · l.8176 · p.255 · new/high

    London: Trübner, 1887; re-issued London: Fifield, 1908 and later; p. 126 source ↗

    Cunning, if it can keep its head above water at all, will beat mere luck unaided by cunning, no matter what start luck may have had, if the race be a fairly long one. Growth is a kind of success which does indeed come to some organisms with less effort than to others, but it cannot be maintained and improved upon without pains and effort.

    Butler, against Darwinian chance, argues that organisms succeed by 'cunning', the effort and memory of the organism, and not by luck. Prynne uses the maxim in a field poem about the 'grass ley', the 'calcium defect' and 'the meal ticket'. There growth is the farm economy's measure of success, and the question 'How do / they get in if not by straying' is about weeds or pests coming in. Butler's Lamarckian claim that organisms earn their growth is set against an agriculture whose yields are forced by chemistry, and where 'the atrophy continues' as the poem goes on.

    quotation. kbgrep 'Luck or Cunning', 'Luck, or Cunning', 'growth is a kind of success': no hits. Corroboration: on 20 July 1975 Prynne wrote to Dorn enthusing about Charles Creighton's Illustrations of Unconscious Memory in Disease (1886). Butler's Luck or Cunning praises and quotes that book at length (ch. on Romanes, pp. 68 ff.), so Prynne was reading in this Butler-Creighton circle in 1975.

    Verified: inside.py 'growth is a kind of success' gave 9 hits, all Luck or Cunning (several printings) except Prynne and a 2000s CLEP guide. I read the passage in the IA djvu text (p. 126).

    In Propertius I.8 the poet imagines Cynthia sailing off to Illyria with a rival. He is left 'fixed upon the vacant foreshore', calling her cruel. Prynne splits the elegy across his poem: first 'the small boat at sea a noted / twist of cruelty', then 'your same little boat, / pulling away from the vacant foreshore'. The '51Cr label' that shows 'them and us in your same little boat' turns the lover's lament into a tracer experiment.

  214. The distance (2) from a self
    protein is not by nature
    either just or rational but
    the mirror image of both.     Thomas Traherne, Christian Ethicks High Pink on Chrome (1975) · High Pink on Chrome: 'The distance (2) from a self' · l.8242 · p.258 · new/high

    London, 1675; ed. C. L. Marks and G. R. Guffey (Ithaca: Cornell UP, 1968); modernised as The Way to Blessedness, ed. Margaret Bottrall (London, 1962); ch. XXV ('Of Meekness') source ↗

    For by Nature we are to be Just and Good towards all that are Innocent, and kind to all those to whom Kindness is due: but it is not by Nature either just or rational that we should love any Creature that is Evil: and how GOD came to do it first is an infinite Wonder.

    Traherne says that loving what is evil goes beyond nature and reason, and that this is the 'infinite Wonder' of grace. Prynne moves the sentence into immunology: the 'distance ... from a self protein' is the margin by which an immune system tells self from non-self. That margin is the subject of Turk's account, quoted in poem 7, of metal-modified 'body's own proteins' attacked by the body. Neither justice nor reason sets that boundary, so autoimmunity becomes a parody of Traherne's love of the unlovable: the body cannot tell its own altered substance from an enemy.

    adaptation. kbgrep 'Traherne', 'Christian Ethicks', 'either just or rational': no hits. Prynne quotes Traherne's verse to Olson (31 Jan 1966), so he knew the author, but no critic has linked Christian Ethicks to High Pink.

    Verified: Found by an n-gram match against the IA djvu text of the 1675 edition (running head 'Of Meekness'). inside.py with the item identifier confirms identical wording in the 1968 Cornell edition and in Bottrall's 1962 modernised text. The phrase 'not by nature either just or rational' is verbatim.

Prynne splits the confession and puts in 'across the somatic metal / shifting', so that the inexpressible becomes a symptom: something in the bone, the radiological 'critical organ', that the speaker cannot account for. Five lines later the poem lifts a sentence from a few lines earlier in the same paragraph (see line 8313), so Prynne quotes the passage in reverse order.

This poem has a closing quotation mark after 'explain' but no opening one. The lift accounts for the stray mark.

  216. What right to work, if there is

    Traherne argues that God gave creatures freedom, even freedom to sin, because love and wisdom must be chosen. Prynne asks 'What right to work' against this, which is a labour-politics phrase (the 'right to work'). It sits beside 'clip and fold the patch-work / of the new-born': if wisdom needs a voluntary act, compelled labour and exposure without consent (the poisoned and the treated) have no wisdom in them. The poem uses the Caroline theology of free will to measure how unfree its toxic and economic scene is.

    Willmer was a Cambridge physiologist, and his book argues for cell lineages across evolution. The sentence is about the hard question of where the vertebrate coelom comes from. Prynne cuts it to a flat avowal of ignorance and places it between 'Dead right you are as you bleed' and Hammond's 'a great latitude in prudence'. The obscurity of the body's inner cavity, where blood and poison spread ('access by / blood spread'), stands for what the toxic scene cannot see into. The textbook register is kept exact, so the poem's last moral judgements meet a gap in scientific knowledge.

  220. There is
    a great latitude in prudence.     Henry Hammond, Of Will-Worship (1644) High Pink on Chrome (1975) · High Pink on Chrome: 'Now the band narrows towards' · l.8356 · p.263 · new/high

    Severall Tracts (London, 1646); Workes, vol. 1 (London, 1674); Of Will-Worship, sect. 42 source ↗

    This is the last poem of the sequence. It closes on a moral maxim that grants room for manoeuvre ('latitude'), set just after an emergency dose ('dimercaprol 200 mg') and an embryology sentence lifted from Willmer. Read as Hammond's clause, the line does not plead caution. It says that how much one gives is not fixed by duty, which in a poem about poison and its antidote is a concession at once humane and chilling. In the same poem the 'charm of love amongst men' is also from Hammond. Together they make the poem's ethical vocabulary that of Caroline casuistry.

  222. "The sun does not rise upon our countrymen; our land is little cheered by its beams; we are contented with that twilight, which, among you, precedes the sun-rise, or follows the sun-set. Moreover, a certain luminous country is seen, not far distant from ours, and divided from it by a very considerable river." William of Newburgh, trans. Joseph Stevenson, Historia rerum Anglicarum (The History of William of Newburgh), Book I, ch. 27 ('Of the green children') The Land of Saint Martin (1976) · The Land of Saint Martin · l.8367 · p.266 · partial/high

    The Church Historians of England, vol. IV, part II (London: Seeleys, 1856); p. 437 source ↗

    "The sun does not rise upon our countrymen; our land is little cheered by its beams; we are contented with that twilight, which, among you, precedes the sun-rise, or follows the sun-set. Moreover, a certain luminous country is seen, not far distant from ours, and divided from it by a very considerable river." These, and many other matters, too numerous to particularize, they are said to have recounted to curious inquirers.

    The epigraph is not Prynne's paraphrase but an exact copy of the standard Victorian translation, so its stiff Latinate English ('little cheered by its beams', 'a very considerable river') belongs to the 1856 translator. That fact matters for the sequence, which is about learning a language. In Newburgh the children speak these words only after they 'learnt our language', and they speak them through a translator's idiom twice removed from them. The monosyllabic stanzas that follow put the reader at the children's stage of acquisition, with the finished period of the epigraph as the 'luminous country' across the river. Stevenson's next sentence ('These, and many other matters, too numerous to particularize') shows that the epigraph is cut from a longer testimony that the chronicler himself breaks off.

    quotation. N. H. Reeve, 'Twilight Zones' (English 51, 2002; bib-59d74520bf) tracks the epigraph to William of Newburgh but calls it 'a fairly free rendering into English' and quotes a different, modern translation. He does not identify Stevenson's 1856 version, which Prynne copies exactly. Eltringham (2018) also cites the Woolpit legend. No other kbgrep hits for 'Stevenson' in this context.

    Verified: Read the full passage in the archive.org djvu text of Stevenson (item churchhistorians0006revj). The epigraph is word-for-word and punctuation-for-punctuation Stevenson, including the hyphenated 'sun-rise' and 'sun-set' and the parenthetic 'among you'. inside.py and olinside.py ('a certain luminous country', 'contented with that twilight') before 1977 find only Stevenson (1853/1856 printings) and H. T. Wilkins (1959), whose paraphrase differs ('not warmed by the beams of the sun'). Later verbatim reprints (Carey, Faber Book of Reportage, 1987) postdate the poem.

  223. Between two states run the waters
    of the river no man steps into but

    DK B12/B91; Plato, Cratylus 402a; no specific translation; fr. 41 source ↗

    You cannot step twice into the same rivers; for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you.

    Prynne reduces the paradox to a joke about children. The river 'no man steps into' (twice) is where 'the smalls' (Prynne's family word for children, also in his letters) splash every day without thinking. The river of flux 'between two states' becomes a frontier as well ('a civil order intently crossed'), so the line divides the philosopher's man, who cannot re-enter the river, from the children, who are always in it.
