  224. Consulto Speculo geris Omnia; fallet Imago:
    Te nam (an jurares) sera Ruina manet.     Edward Benlowes, Theophila, or Loves Sacrifice (1652), Canto XI 'The Vanity of the World': Latin verses 'In lenocitantes hujus Tempestatis Venerillas, Juvenum Scrobes, Animarum Voragines' News of Warring Clans (1977) · News of Warring Clans · l.8547 · p.276 · known/high

    George Saintsbury, ed., Minor Poets of the Caroline Period, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1905); p. 440, ll. 31-32 of the Latin poem; Benlowes's note on l. 32: 'Versus cancrinus quoad Literas' source ↗

    Sidera contendas Oculi sint, Purpura Malas, / Electrum Crines, Dens Ebur, Ora Favi. / Consulto Speculo geris Omnia; fallet Imago: / Te nam (an jurares) sera Ruina manet. [note: Versus cancrinus quoad Literas]

    The couplet closes Benlowes's satire on the painted, patched 'Venerillas' of his time. In it, eyes, cheeks, hair and teeth are bought as stars, purple, amber and ivory: 'you put everything on by consulting the mirror; the image will deceive; for (would you swear otherwise?) late ruin awaits you'. The second line is a letter-palindrome (Benlowes's 'versus cancrinus'), so it reads the same in the mirror. In News of Warring Clans the cosmetic context returns as war paint ('Four dark lines on the lower cheek then / stubbed at the nose bridge', l. 8577), as 'Cosmetic universals' (l. 8717), and in the Jonson song on painted ladies a few lines later (l. 8721). The epigraph therefore introduces the poem's theme: a face made for the glass that the glass will betray. That is the same deception the poem finds in its 'lying report' and 'stylish lies'.

    quotation. Kevin Nolan, 'Capital Calves' (Jacket 24, 2003; bib-45909937c8) names 'the palindromic epigraph from Edward Benlowes' and reads it through the Pauline speculum. Stephen Hardy (Brno Studies in English, 2016; bib-ee403bce77) cites Theophila in Saintsbury. Neither discusses the poem the couplet comes from: Benlowes's satire on face-painting women.

    Verified: Read the context in the archive.org djvu text of Saintsbury vol. I (minorpoetsofcar01sain). Prynne's capitals and punctuation match Saintsbury exactly. Saintsbury's footnote says the original has at this point a Hollar plate of 'a lady with a fan... her face and neck spotted with sign-patches as in the Latin verses'. Falconer Madan, Oxford Books (1895), also notes the palindrome.

  225. emotional
    negativism and fatuous serenity are states     James W. Papez, A Proposed Mechanism of Emotion News of Warring Clans (1977) · News of Warring Clans · l.8553 · p.276 · new/high

    Archives of Neurology and Psychiatry 38 (1937), 725-743; reprinted in R. L. Isaacson (ed.), Basic Readings in Neuropsychology (New York: Harper & Row, 1964); Isaacson 1964, IA leaf n454 source ↗

    Hart remarked that "emotional negativism and fatuous serenity are states of mind described by numerous authors ..."

    Papez's paper is the founding statement of the limbic 'Papez circuit', the proposal that emotion is generated by a closed loop of hypothalamus, thalamus, cingulate gyrus and hippocampus. Its quotation from Hart lists the emotional states produced by lesions near the third ventricle. Prynne lifts the clinical clause into the clan's 'prehistory', where a 'panic' about completion is answered by states that are pathologies, not virtues; his next words, 'like a loose rein on quite the wrong horse', turn the neurological picture of affect without control into an image of misdirected command. It extends the book's neurology (the 'dizygotic twins', 'blood group', Watson and Crick) to the anatomy of feeling itself.

    quotation. kbgrep 'Papez' and 'fatuous serenity': no hits in the criticism corpus.

    Verified: Surfaced by the date-filtered Internet Archive sweep (score 12.7); the six-word run checked in the 1937 Archives scan and in Isaacson 1964 by in-item search, which also names the reprinted paper (Papez, 'A Proposed Mechanism of Emotion'). 'Emotional negativism' alone is in general use (115 IA hits), but the full run occurs only in Papez and its reprints (lead review).

  226. The incidence of dizygotic twins is in unexplained decline*. J. M. Elwood; W. H. James (correspondence), 'Decline in dizygotic twinning' News of Warring Clans (1977) · News of Warring Clans · l.8602 · p.277 · new/medium

    New England Journal of Medicine 288-289 (1973), letters; cf. James, 'The secular decline in dizygotic twinning rates in Italy', Acta Genet. Med. Gemellol. (1975); NEJM 1973 index, 'Twins. Decline in dizygotic twinning [Elwood] ... (cont.) [James]' source ↗

    Twins. Decline in dizygotic twinning [Elwood] ... Decline in dizygotic twinning (cont.) [James]

    The line, marked off by Prynne's asterisk, reports a real epidemiological puzzle of the early 1970s: in Europe, North America and Japan the rate of dizygotic (non-identical) twinning had been falling since the 1950s without agreed cause (hormones, nutrition and contraception were proposed). Prynne attributes it at once to 'a lapsed sibling policy', so a demographic statistic becomes the clan's failed kinship planning, beside the genetic vocabulary of the Watson-Crick and 'central dogma' lifts later in the poem.

    allusion. Not identified in the criticism corpus; an earlier hunt agent left the line unverified.

    Verified: inside.py 'decline in dizygotic twinning' before 1978: 11 hits, all medical journals and reports of 1973-76 (NEJM, BMJ, UCL report, Ziegler 1976) on the secular fall in DZ twin rates, whose cause was then unknown. No verbatim source for Prynne's sentence was found (lead review).

  227. Option trading has become
    the hottest game in town.     financial-press tag, 1975-77, 'the hottest game in town' (stock options) News of Warring Clans (1977) · News of Warring Clans · l.8653 · p.279 · new/medium

    e.g. Medical Economics (1975), 'Stock options: the hottest game in town'; Engel & Wyckoff (1977) chapter title; an F&S Index abstract of the NYT, 8 Aug 1976; NYT 8 Aug 1976, p. F3 source ↗

    Options trading has become the hottest game in town @NY Times 8/8/76 pF3

    The line is a 1975-77 press cliché about the new Chicago options market, set into the poem without quotation marks, and the 'game' is real. In the passage, 'All risks / are no risk' gives the hedging rationale of options, and the journalist's breezy idiom is then corrupted by the clan's 'tribal actuary'. Because the borrowing comes from the business pages, the poem's subject is the news coverage of a market as well as the market. This fits the 'news' of the title.

    echo. Pietrzak, Levity of Design (2012; kb bib-9a5bd81a75, mislabelled) and Stanley (2021) quote the line but do not identify it as financial journalism. No kbgrep hits for 'hottest game' besides those quotations.

    Verified: Seen as an index entry in the F&S Index (1977) on archive.org. I could not see the NYT page itself, because nytimes.com refuses the fetch. The phrase was a financial-press tag in 1973-77: Medical Economics (13 Oct 1975), 'Stock options: the hottest game in town'; Engel & Wyckoff, How to Buy Stocks (1976/77), chapter heading 'Playing "The Hottest Game in Town"—Options'; Time (1975), 'options trading has become the hottest securities game around'. Prynne's sentence matches the NYT wording word for word except for 'Option' for 'Options'.

  228. And does the option
    wag the stock, with peace and gentle visitation?
    ...
    what you say it does, messenger creature.     William Shakespeare, Love's Labour's Lost News of Warring Clans (1977) · News of Warring Clans · l.8656 · p.279 · new/high

    Project Gutenberg #1510; V.ii.177-180 (the Muscovite masque) source ↗

    BOYET. What would you with the Princess? / BEROWNE. Nothing but peace and gentle visitation. / ROSALINE. What would they, say they? / BOYET. Nothing but peace and gentle visitation.

    In the source, the King and his lords visit the Princess disguised as Muscovites, and their professed 'peace and gentle visitation' is a masked seduction. Boyet, the go-between, repeats it word for word as the women make fun of the wooers. Prynne's 'messenger creature' five lines later identifies Boyet's role: what reaches us is 'what you say it does', the courier's relay of a disguised claim. So the option that 'wags the stock' arrives in the costume of courtly peace, and the masque of false foreigners fits the poem's clans, who wear paint and speak by cypher.

    quotation. Pietrzak (2012) and Stanley (2021) both quote this line and read it as journalistic or financial irony. Neither identifies Shakespeare. kbgrep 'gentle visitation' and 'Labour's Lost' give no other hits.

    Verified: Read in the Gutenberg text. inside.py 'peace and gentle visitation' gives Shakespeare editions only (Wordsworth has 'gentle visitation' without 'peace'). The phrase is spoken twice, the second time by the messenger Boyet relaying it.

  229. For all around
    the cool breeze murmurs, rustling through branches,
    while from shivering leaves and broken lights
    streams down deep sleep, lying where it falls.     Sappho, trans. Edwin Marion Cox, Sappho fr. 2 (Lobel-Page; fr. 4/5 Bergk), the 'apple-branch' fragment News of Warring Clans (1977) · News of Warring Clans · l.8694 · p.280 · new/high

    E. M. Cox, Sappho and the Sapphic Metre in English (London: privately printed, 1916); p. 21 source ↗

    And all around, the cool breeze murmurs, rustling / Through apple branches, while from quivering leaves, / Streams down deep slumber.

    The only lyric passage in the poem is a Sappho translation, but Prynne has stripped the sacred grove of its apple trees. Cox's note on this fragment praises the 'drowsy cadence' of κῶμα καταρρεῖ, a sleep 'deeper, with a quality of oblivion in it'. Prynne puts this oblivion directly after 'fate stands / fixed on the canteen floor' and before 'the song & dance of a small minority', so the classical locus amoenus serves as the narcotic that the clan sinks into. 'Shivering leaves and broken lights' brings cold and fracture into Sappho's shimmering shade. 'Lying where it falls' turns the sleep into a casualty and puns on the poem's continuous 'lying' (the 'lying report', 'stylish lies').

    adaptation. kbgrep 'cool breeze murmurs', 'shivering leaves', and Sappho together with this poem give no hits. A web search for Prynne + News of Warring Clans + Sappho finds nothing.

    Verified: Read in the archive.org djvu text of Cox (1916) (sapphosapphicmet00coxe), where Cox gives the Greek and calls this his 'fairly close translation'. inside.py 'all around, the cool breeze' matches only Cox 1916 and Prynne. Cox revised the version in The Poems of Sappho (1924/25) to 'By the cool water the breeze murmurs, rustling / Through apple branches', and that revised form is the one in Goldsmith (1938), the Peter Pauper anthology (1942), and Rexroth's 'The Poet as Translator' (Assays, 1961). Prynne's 'all around... the cool breeze murmurs, rustling... while from... leaves... streams down deep' therefore follows the 1916 text. He drops 'apple', changes 'quivering' to 'shivering' and 'slumber' to 'sleep', and adds 'and broken lights' and 'lying where it falls'.

  230. And still to be dressed, still to be neat
    is truth or riot in the street,
    Floating like the oil upon
    the chartered streams of Babylon.     Ben Jonson, Epicoene, or The Silent Woman (1609), I.i, the Page's song 'Still to be neat, still to be drest' News of Warring Clans (1977) · News of Warring Clans · l.8721 · p.280 · new/high

    Project Gutenberg #4011 (from the Gifford/Cunningham text); Act I, scene i source ↗

    [Clerimont:] ...till she has painted, and perfumed, and wash'd, and scour'd, but the boy here; and him she wipes her oil'd lips upon, like a sponge. I have made a song, I pray thee hear it, on the subject. / Still to be neat, still to be drest, / As you were going to a feast; / Still to be powder'd, still perfum'd; / Lady, it is to be presumed, / Though art's hid causes are not found, / All is not sweet, all is not sound. / ... [Truewit:] ...take often counsel of her glass, and choose the best... paint, and profess it.

    Jonson's song attacks a lady's painting and perfuming ('all the adulteries of art'). Clerimont introduces it with her 'oil'd lips', and Truewit answers that a woman should 'take often counsel of her glass... paint, and profess it'. That answer is the 'Consulto Speculo' of Benlowes's epigraph in English. Prynne's inserted quatrain, the poem's one rhymed set piece, thus confirms that the epigraph's anti-cosmetic satire runs through the poem. Jonson's 'oil'd lips' become oil floating on the rivers of a mercantile Babylon (see the next finding), so that cosmetic 'neatness' is joined to the oil economy that Stanley sees behind the poem. Jonson's line 'All is not sweet, all is not sound' prepares the turn to 'truth or riot in the street'.

    adaptation. kbgrep 'still to be neat', 'still to be dressed', 'Epicoene' give no hits. Stanley (2021) quotes 'the chartered streams of Babylon' as a Middle Eastern reference and does not mention Jonson.

    Verified: Read Act I scene i in the Gutenberg text. Prynne's line swaps the order of Jonson's two phrases and keeps his tetrameter couplet form for the four-line insert.

  231. the chartered streams of Babylon William Blake; Psalm 137, 'London', Songs of Experience (1794); Psalm 137:1 'By the rivers of Babylon' News of Warring Clans (1977) · News of Warring Clans · l.8728 · p.281 · new/medium

    Blake, Poems (Project Gutenberg #1934); 'London', ll. 1-2 source ↗

    I wander through each chartered street, / Near where the chartered Thames does flow,

    Blake's 'chartered' means streets and river owned by charter and commerce. Prynne moves his London river to Babylon, the psalm's place of exile and the Apocalypse's city of merchants. The oil that floats on the streams is both Jonson's cosmetic oil and petroleum. The 'street' and 'streams' pair keeps Blake's hint that commerce controls even natural flow, and this is joined to the 'truth or riot in the street' of 1970s unrest.

    allusion. kbgrep 'chartered streams' gives only Stanley (2021), who quotes the phrase as an allusion to the Middle East and does not mention Blake.

    Verified: Read in the Gutenberg Blake text. Prynne's 'street' rhyme two lines earlier ('riot in the street') with 'chartered streams' reproduces Blake's chartered street / chartered Thames pair.

  232. Several coal and marble mines are already
    reported to have been seized.     news reports of the Baluchi rising (May 1973), e.g. as summarised in Facts on File News of Warring Clans (1977) · News of Warring Clans · l.8757 · p.281 · new/medium

    not a located text; Pakistan: Baluchistan revolt source ↗

    ...was further heightened by the seizure of coal and marble mines by rebellious workers. Baluchistan officials charged May 19 that ... The insurgent elements, members of the Marri and Mengal tribes, were said to have set fire to telephone ...

    The sentence is a news report of the Baluchi tribal rising against Bhutto's government (1973-77): tribal sardars, the Marri and Mengal clans, the seizure of mines. The same poem names 'Kalat' ('north & west of Kalat, two miles out of Kendal'). The title's 'warring clans' therefore has a real referent in contemporary news, and Prynne moves it into an English landscape. Prynne's letter to Dorn of 16 Aug. 1977 mentions a television film about north-west Pakistan. Reading 'Kalat' as the Baluchi town is probable, not proven (Qalat is also in Afghanistan). In a letter to Dorn of 16 Aug. 1977 Prynne describes a TV travel film about north-west Pakistan and uses the phrase 'Hunting Clan'.

    allusion. kbgrep 'Baluch', 'marble mines': none. Joshua Stanley (Textual Practice 2021) reads the poem's 'Kalat' as an Iranian town. Kalat is the Baluchi princely state and district at the centre of the 1973-77 insurgency.

    Verified: inside.py 'coal and marble mines' (before 1979) gave only one modern hit, Facts on File 1973. I read its snippets inside the item: the seizure of coal and marble mines in the Baluchistan rising of 1973 (Marri and Mengal tribes; Governor Bizenjo and Chief Minister Ataullah Mengal dismissed in Feb. 1973). The newspaper or wire wording that Prynne copies ('are already reported to have been seized') was not found. The Times on IA has no 1973 hit.

  233. the purest
    central dogma in the history of trash.     F. H. C. Crick, 'On Protein Synthesis', Symposia of the Society for Experimental Biology 12 (1958): 138-63 News of Warring Clans (1977) · News of Warring Clans · l.8770 · p.282 · new/medium

    quoted in H. Quastler, The Emergence of Biological Organization (1964); p. 153 source ↗

    The Central Dogma. This states that once 'information' has passed into protein it cannot get out again.

    Crick's 'dogma' says that information flows one way and cannot return. As 'the purest / central dogma in the history of trash', it describes a culture in which good taste is 'reconstructed as billboard nostalgia', and the copy cannot get back to an original. Together with the Watson-Crick quotation that follows, it gives the clan's lying reports the authority of a law of heredity.

    allusion. kbgrep 'central dogma' gives Pietrzak (2012), who quotes the line without the biological sense, and other unrelated Prynne items (Middleton 2009 on scientific language; Prynne's Stars, Tigers lectures). None links this line to Crick.

    Verified: Crick's formulation seen in inside.py snippets (Quastler 1964; Braverman 1973). The term is Crick's and was standard in molecular biology by 1977. Its position three lines before the Watson-Crick quotation supports the link.

  234. "it has not escaped our notice" that, by
    song & dance, men cannot live or move out
    in the midst of plenty.     J. D. Watson and F. H. C. Crick, 'Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid' News of Warring Clans (1977) · News of Warring Clans · l.8773 · p.282 · new/high

    Nature 171 (25 April 1953): 737-38; quoted again in Watson, The Double Helix (1968); p. 737 source ↗

    It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.

    The coy close of the double-helix paper announces, without seeming to, a mechanism for self-copying. Prynne puts this rhetoric of discovery in front of a parody of Deuteronomy 8:3 / Matthew 4:4 ('man doth not live by bread only'), and 'planned parenthood', 'clone', 'sibling policy', 'dizygotic twins' and 'blood group' surround it. The clan's genetic reproduction and its economic reproduction ('the purest / central dogma', three lines earlier) are thus voiced in the idiom of molecular biology's founding paper.

    quotation. Pietrzak, Levity of Design (2012, pp. 82-83) says these inverted-comma words are 'impossible to trace because such words are spoken on a daily basis by everyone'. kbgrep 'not escaped our notice' gives only that passage. The attribution corrects him.

    Verified: Seen in inside.py snippets of the 1953 paper (archive.org item B-001-004-394) and of The Double Helix (1968). The quotation marks in Prynne mark the lift. This is the most famous understatement in twentieth-century science. The phrase alone is common (240 pre-1978 hits); the attribution rests on Prynne's quotation marks, the adjacent 'central dogma' and the poem's genetic vocabulary.

  235. men cannot live or move out
    in the midst of plenty     William Morris, as quoted by E. P. Thompson, 'A Socialist Poet on Bombs and Anarchism' (interview, Justice, 27 January 1894), quoted in E. P. Thompson, William Morris: Romantic to Revolutionary News of Warring Clans (1977) · News of Warring Clans · l.8774 · p.282 · new/high

    London: Lawrence & Wishart, 1955; revised edn London: Merlin, 1977; rev. edn 1977, Part IV, section ii 'Goodbye to the anarchists' (pp. 585-96), last paragraph before section iii 'The rejection of purism' (p. 597); IA leaf n854 source ↗

    Anarchism, as a theory, negatives society, and puts man outside it. Now, man is unthinkable outside society. Man cannot live or move outside it. This negation of society is the position taken up by the logical Anarchists ...

    Prynne takes Morris's sentence against the anarchists and cuts it at the line break, so that 'outside' becomes 'out / in the midst of plenty'. Morris states as a social axiom that man is unthinkable outside society. In the poem that axiom becomes a statement about entrapment inside consumer abundance ('We munch and munch / along planned parenthood, getting and spending / on the same credit card'). In this poem of clans, raids and 'tribal' order, the line borrows the founding claim of socialist communalism and makes it the condition of the 'song & dance' economy. It also fixes this axiom to Watson and Crick's scientific understatement, which comes just before it. The phrase 'live or move' also keeps the Pauline echo in Morris's sentence (Acts 17:28, 'in him we live, and move, and have our being'). The lift therefore puts a theological ground under the lost 'outside'.

    adaptation. kbgrep 'cannot live or move', 'unthinkable outside' and 'Romantic to Revolutionary' match only the text of the poem (the English Intelligencer/bibliography entry that reproduces it). The prior entry for 8773 gives only Watson & Crick for the quoted formula and does not account for 'men cannot live or move out'. A web search for Prynne with Morris or Thompson found nothing.

    Verified: inside.py 'Men cannot live or move' (no year) returns only Prynne (Poems 1982; Sulfur 23) and a book that quotes Morris (P. Meier, William Morris: The Marxist Dreamer, 1978). 'cannot live or move outside' returns Thompson's William Morris in the 1955/1961, 1977, 1988 and 2011 printings and books that quote it from Thompson. Searches inside the 1977 Merlin edition (williammorris00epth) give 'Anarchism, as a theory, negatives society, and puts man outside it. Now, man is unthinkable outside society. Man cannot live or move outside it.' The table of contents gives section ii 'Goodbye to the anarchists (585)' and iii 'The rejection of purism (597)'. olinside.py places the quotation on leaf n854. The same leaf carries the Hammersmith 'Vestry' election passage ('the Vestry candidates were defeated: "You see all through London the middle class voted solid against ..."'). Prynne's 'Good taste was shunted into the slogan vestry' comes four lines before his 'men cannot live or move out'. The interview's title and date are from Knepper (2010) and Forman, The Books of William Morris, which cite it.

    The poem's title, 'Stay Where You Are', matches Pope's ode on contented staying at home, but the ode's rural sufficiency is now package tourism: 'the rest camp you pay to leave, / long to fly over'. Suckling's language of debt (bankrupt, wherewithal, pay) fits Prynne's run of commercial phrases ('reasonable commodity', 'make good', 'deal'). The verbatim Plato a few lines later gives the same poem a second winged-soul source.

The image, the imitation, and the trapping are one process. The candle-light netting of a Lincolnshire fowling custom sits next to soda ash, flash-cured bacon and lime slurry, which are fenland and Norfolk industrial-agricultural products.     The city walls, shattered, shall everywhere fall, the mountains shall melt and the high cliffs ...     The Old English apocalypse gives the paradox that even water burns, 'like wax', in the fire that ends creation. Prynne lifts it into a weather-forecast idiom ('shut down and frontal', 'storm perpetual') and a municipal one ('paid by turn', 'byelaw'). The cluster around the lift corresponds to the source: Brooke's 'the stun and the storm' becomes 'storm perpetual', the 'fyrswearta leg' (fire-swart flame) becomes 'this darkened flame', and 'the mountains shall melt' becomes the flame that will 'melt the byelaw'. Doomsday is reduced to the grumble 'you say'. The total dissolution of creation is set against a small local rule, and in this collection, full of broken-down transport and public utilities, this fits an apocalypse of ordinary administration.

  255. Or, when a lark
    while over the sea
    blindly following
    its instinct to ascend
    into the air, and
    to fall again
    descends to
    the sea, and
    is drowned.     Johann August Unzer (tr. Thomas Laycock), The Principles of Physiology Down where changed (1979) · Down where changed: 'Or, when a lark' · l.9275 · p.295 · new/high

    The Principles of Physiology by John Augustus Unzer, and A Dissertation on the Functions of the Nervous System by George Prochaska, tr. and ed. Thomas Laycock (London: Sydenham Society, 1851); Part I, ch. III ('Actions of instincts'), §266, pp. 134-35 source ↗

    as, for example, when a hen, which has trod upon her chicken, hearing its cry, calls it to some food, without at the same time lifting its foot ; or when a lobster having one of its legs fixed in and pinched by one of its claws, excited by the pain, violently tears away the limb, instead of opening its claw ; or, when a lark, while over the sea, blindly following its instinct to ascend into the air, and to fall again, descends to the sea, and is drowned.

    The poem's opening 'Or,' is not a lyric gesture. It is a list item from an 18th-century physiology of reflex and instinct, which Laycock translated in 1851 as a founding text of reflex theory. In Unzer the lark is the last of three examples of 'the stupidity of animals': a hen standing on her chick, a lobster tearing off its own leg, a lark that drowns. Each shows a sentient instinct carried out blindly, in an action that defeats its own purpose. Prynne removes the frame and leaves the bare case, so the Romantic emblem of the ascending lark (Shelley, Meredith, Vaughan Williams) becomes a mechanism that sends the bird into the sea. This suits a sequence about 'no choice but one', habit, and compulsion. The 'battery hen' and 'hen level' later in the sequence may be a second echo of Unzer's list, but they are too common to claim.

An n-gram pass of the whole sequence against the Unzer text finds no other borrowing.

The surviving verbatim printings are dated 1980, so Prynne probably met it in an earlier circulated paper or the press, and this keeps the confidence at medium. The poem puts the formula after an NHS operating theatre ('introit', 'Trauersaft', the vase that 'shatters softly'). The promise of systemic leverage is thus juxtaposed with the patient's body, and the stanza ends on a decline ('it comes apace / it comes amiss / it comes too late').

The 'stupid creep / under the stairs' hear only a shallow summons, so they 'fail the test, and miss our doom'. The parody hymn is about an air-raid or fallout shelter ('under the stairs', 'in the gloom', 'to fall asleep'), so the change is bitter: shelter replaces the abyss of the psalm, and the doom is missed and not met.

  260. The consumption of any product
    is the destruction of its value
    thus the land is cleared     Charles Knight, Knowledge is Power: a View of the Productive Forces of Modern Society, and the Results of Labour, Capital, and Skill Down where changed (1979) · Down where changed: 'The consumption of any product' · l.9424 · p.308 · new/high

    London: John Murray, 1855 (and later editions); the sentence first appears in the Penny Cyclopaedia, vol. 1 (1833), and the clearing passage that follows it is from Knight's The Rights of Industry (1831; repr. as Capital and Labour, 1845); ch. IV ('Features of accumulation'), pp. 41-42 source ↗

    The consumption of any production is the destruction of its value. The production was created by industry to administer to individual wants, to be consumed, to be destroyed. [...] It may assist us in making the value of capital more clear, if we take a rapid view of the most obvious features of the accumulation of a highly civilized country. The first operation in a newly settled country is what is termed to clear it. Look at a civilized country, such as England. It is cleared. The encumbering woods are cut down, the unhealthy marshes are drained.

    Knight was the 'useful knowledge' publisher of the 1830s. His sentence is from a passage praising accumulation: consumption destroys value, so only savings, capital and the clearing of land let civilisation advance. In his account England's clearing is a triumph: woods cut down, marshes drained, 'noxious animals' exterminated. Prynne takes the axiom and the clearing and leaves out the progress narrative that justified them. 'Thus' becomes a cold logical step, and the clearing is done 'by the footprint of a quiet man / with a snack in his wife's pocket', so every small act of consumption takes part. Wilkinson reads the stanza as 'no possibility of exculpation for even the gentlest of earth's beneficiaries'. The source supports that reading, because Prynne uses Victorian political economy's optimistic proof against itself. The sequence's one-word line 'rubbish' and Prynne's interest in Thompson's Rubbish Theory (1978-79) make the economics of value-destruction a deliberate theme.

    adaptation. kbgrep 'destruction of its value': only Wilkinson ('Heigh Ho', Glossator 2) and Jow Lindsay's blog, who both quote the poem with no source. kbgrep 'Charles Knight', 'Knowledge is Power', 'Penny Cyclop': 0. The web finds no attribution. Context: Prynne's letter to Dorn of 25 August 1978 encloses a publisher's flyer for Michael Thompson's Rubbish Theory: The Creation and Destruction of Value (1979). A search inside the IA copy of Thompson does not find Knight's sentence, so Thompson was not the conduit.

    Verified: inside.py 'is the destruction of its value' (before 1980) gives 12 hits. Apart from one unrelated sermon, all are Knight's Knowledge is Power (1855-66 printings) or the Penny Cyclopaedia vol. 1 (1833). Read in the djvu text of knowledgeispower00knigrich, ch. IV, pp. 41-42. There, two sentences after the sentence about value, the next paragraph is the 'clear it ... It is cleared' passage, which gives Prynne's 'thus the land is cleared'. Prynne changes 'production' to 'product'. 'Consumption is the destruction of value' (Say, Wayland) is a commonplace of classical economics. But the exact form 'of any ... is the destruction of its value' is Knight's, and Knight's next paragraph is about clearing land.

  261. BEFORE is a relation, of degree two, but it is
    a relation for which not all the underlying
    domains are simple. AFTER is a semantically
    equivalent relation of degree three, with the
    property that all its domains are simple—in
    other words, AFTER is normalized.     C. J. Date, An Introduction to Database Systems The Oval Window (1983) · The Oval Window · l.9488 · p.312 · partial/high

    3rd edn (Addison-Wesley, 1981); wording possibly also in the 2nd edn (1977); the 1st edn (1975) differs; discussion of normalization (relations BEFORE and AFTER); page not recovered (lending-only scan) source ↗

    Mathematically speaking, BEFORE is a relation, of degree two, but it is a relation for which not all the underlying domains are simple. (A simple domain is one ...) AFTER is a semantically equivalent relation of degree three, with the property that all its domains are simple— in other words, AFTER is normalized. We choose to support only normalized ...

    The poem opens with a verbatim paragraph from the standard 1981 database textbook, where BEFORE and AFTER are only the names of two example tables, one unnormalized, one normalized. Lifted out, the names become temporal words, so the opening reads as a theorem about time: 'before' has unsimple domains, 'after' has been made simple by decomposition. The technical sense of 'normalized' (repeating groups removed, data made flat and regular) gives a dry, exact model for what the poem fears the present does to experience. Date is the source of three more passages in the poem (views as windows on the real data; the internal view; the domain as a pool of values), so the 'window' of the title has a database sense from the first page.

J. Date', 'Database Systems', 'normalized' in an Oval Window context; web search 'Prynne Oval Window Introduction to Database Systems' finds nothing. Prynne drops only 'Mathematically speaking' and Date's parenthesis defining a simple domain.

  262. This condition says

    given the present,
    the past and future

    Princeton, N.J.: Van Nostrand, 1960; ch. II (definition of a Markov chain); page not recovered source ↗

    This condition says essentially that, given the present, the past and future are independent of each other.

    The second epigraph-block is the textbook statement of the Markov property, broken into short lines. Set beside Date's BEFORE/AFTER it makes the opening a pair of formal definitions of time: in a Markov chain the present screens off the past from the future, so that memory adds nothing to prediction. The poem can be read against this claim, since its lyric material (Dowland, the Hua-chien chi, Wordsworth) is all memory and parting, and its question is whether the 'vantage' of the present can be self-sufficient.

  264. Safe in our hands The Times (Pat Healy, Social Services Correspondent), 'Health Service and the cuts: 1. Patient care and facilities certain to suffer, embattled regions say' The Oval Window (1983) · The Oval Window · l.9535 · p.314 · partial/medium

In the poem the reassurance turns into the voice of a minder or a policeman ('won't cut up rough, at all, pent up / and boil over'), and the health-service promise becomes a threat of control. The Times is the probable conduit for a political slogan; Thatcher's words at the 1982 party conference are usually given as 'the National Health Service is safe with us'.

    The trade report's list (oil, precious stones, aircraft) runs on in Prynne into 'the corpses of men, tigers / fish and pythons, "all in a confused tangle"'. The accounting term for goods whose irregular trade spoils the monthly figures is extended to whatever a disaster leaves behind. The sentence that frames it comes from C. J. Date's 'A view is a window / on the real data' (see the existing entry). The phrase is from the same week's Times as the aerosol attack and the NHS circular.

    THE National Institute of Economic and Social Research used to be known as the Treasury in Exile; it was manned partly by Treasury officials, and its forecasting work, which was very like that of the official side, was useful both as a kind of unofficial window on Treasury policy, through which business could take its lead, and as a check on the Treasury's own work.

    Prynne splices the FT's 'unofficial window' into C. J. Date's definition of a database view ('operations against the view are converted, through ... into operations on the real data'; see the Date entry for l. 9611). Both are windows that let an outsider act on, or anticipate, what happens inside. The column is about that window closing ('In these days of ideology and leaks, roles have changed radically'), and this suits a poem whose title names a window that is 'closed in life'.

  275. Either a point
    object or its image point is said
    to be real when the light propagates
    through it     John Strong, Concepts of Classical Optics The Oval Window (1983) · The Oval Window · l.9631 · p.320 · partial/high

    San Francisco: W. H. Freeman, 1958; ch. XIII, §13-1 'General Considerations', p. 274 source ↗

    Either a point object or its image point is said to be real when the light propagates through it. In this figure a and b represent reflections and refractions ...

    Strong's definition makes reality depend on transmission: a point is 'real' only if light actually passes through it. Prynne finishes the sentence with 'by ash bluff to printed charcoal', so the passing light becomes burning. Strong's book supplies the poem's later optical passages too (the exit window, cascaded magnification, the negative crystal), so its sense of 'real' and 'virtual' images is another frame for what may be seen through a window.

  282. as if there are
    two distinct and mutually exclusive actions
    depending on one test.     Brian W. Kernighan and P. J. Plauger, The Elements of Programming Style The Oval Window (1983) · The Oval Window · l.9671 · p.322 · partial/high

    2nd ed., New York: McGraw-Hill, 1978; ch. 3 'Control Structure', p. 32 source ↗

    Kernighan and Plauger are describing when an IF needs an ELSE: only when one test decides between two exclusive branches. Prynne's 'as if' doubts the model of choice in which every decision is a clean binary branch, and the next line answers with 'Viz, oilseed / is a fashion laid out like data'. This is the first of at least nine borrowings from the book in the poem (see below), which together make the style manual's rules for clear control flow one of the poem's main sources.

  284. a picture is not a window. modernist art-critical dictum (attributed variously to Cocteau, Dubuffet), 'A picture is not a window' The Oval Window (1983) · The Oval Window (section 323) · l.9688 · p.323 · partial/medium

    The sentence is a known quotation: it rejects the Renaissance idea, from Alberti, that a painting is a window onto a scene, in favour of the picture as a flat made thing. Prynne sets it after 'Motor life says the branch office' and before Kernighan and Plauger's definition of recursion. It answers C. J. Date's 'A view is a window / on the real data' (l. 9611): the database view is a window, the picture is not. The poem keeps both claims about windows in play under its title.

Prynne follows it with 'as, / within the chain-guard, cold is the meaning / of heat notably absent', a definition by its own opposite, so that recursion is shown working as a figure of thought. The reflexive procedure fits a poem that keeps defining its window by the window.

    Each phrase is common programming vocabulary, but all of them occur in this one book, which the poem certainly quotes, and they are close together in the poem (lines 9725-9742, 9952). 'Sort and merge' (line 9952), which comes just before 'we need its name', uses the name of a pair of subroutines that the book calls 'correctly coded, but not well designed'. 'looping ahead with do and while' (l. 9737) matches the 2nd edn's 'looping with DO and WHILE'.

  290. As they parted, she heard his horse cry out ... bright moonlight whitens the pear blossom ... calm waves flow onward to the horizon.
    Her wrists shine white like the frosted snow;
    they call each other to the south stream ... Chill shadows
    fall from the topmost eaves, clear waters
    run beside the blossoming peach ... bright moonlight
    floods the steps like a cascade of water.     Lois Fusek (trans.), Among the Flowers: The Hua-chien chi The Oval Window (1983) · The Oval Window · l.9839 · p.330 · partial/high

    New York: Columbia University Press, 1982; various lyrics; pages not recovered (lending-only scan) source ↗

    'As they parted, she heard his horse cry out.'; 'Bright moonlight in the house whitens the pear blossom.'; 'The calm waves flow onward to the horizon.'; 'Her wrists shine white like the frosted snow.'; 'Over the flowers they call each other to the south stream.'; 'Chill shadows fall from the topmost eaves.'; 'Clear waters run beside the blossoming peach.'; 'Bright moonlight floods the steps like a cascade of water.'

    Prynne uses Fusek's English renderings of the tenth-century Shu lyrics (tz'u) without change. Their conventions (the lonely woman, the departed lover, moonlight, blossom, the window) are set beside anatomy ('The oval window is closed in life, / by the foot-piece of the stapes') and Dowland. The lines are complete clauses in a translator's prose, and this explains the 'neatly-contoured phrases' that Reeve & Kerridge observed in the second half of the poem.

    quotation. Not in the criticism corpus or Reeve & Kerridge (1993/1995); but Reeve & Kerridge's The Oval Window: A New Annotated Edition (Bloodaxe, 2018), built from Prynne's source archive, reports sources in optics, anatomy, computer programming and Chinese poetry and was not available to check, so this identification may be recorded there. Li Zhimin (reported by Lucas Klein, Symposium 70, 2016) says Prynne 'borrows many lines from Among the Flowers'; Reeve & Kerridge (1993) heard these lines as Palace Style and pointed to Birrell's Jade Terrace instead.   293. The oval window is closed in life,
    by the foot-piece of the stapes. ... Inside
    this window is the perilymph of the vestibule.     R. J. Last, Anatomy, Regional and Applied The Oval Window (1983) · The Oval Window · l.9855 · p.331 · partial/high

    5th edn, London: Churchill Livingstone, 1972 (same wording in the 7th edn, 1984); section on the middle ear, medial wall of the tympanic cavity (1984 edn: leaf n658) source ↗

    Behind and above the promontory is an oval window, the fenestra vestibuli, closed in life by the foot-piece of the stapes. Inside this window is the perilymph of the vestibule. At the bottom of ... (the 1972 IA OCR splits 'peri lymph')

    The title phrase comes from a surgical students' regional anatomy, where the oval window is the membrane-sealed opening between the middle ear and the fluid-filled inner ear. 'Closed in life' is the anatomist's way of saying that the opening is open only in the dry skull. Prynne's comma, 'closed in life, / by the foot-piece', lets the clause read as an existential statement: the window is shut for as long as one lives. This ties into the sequence's motifs of hearing and being deaf to meaning, and of a window that is never transparent. Last's habit of pairing two windows, oval and round, each with fluid 'inside', also suits the poem's play on screens, views and windows.

    quotation. Not in the criticism corpus; Reeve & Kerridge's annotated edition (2018), built from Prynne's archive, may record it (not available). kbgrep 'foot-piece of the stapes' and 'Regional and Applied' found nothing. Punter (2002) quotes the poem's line and explains perilymph but names no source. A web search ('Prynne' 'Oval Window' 'foot-piece of the stapes') found nothing. The 2018 Reeve & Kerridge annotated edition was not checked.

    Verified: inside.py 'in life by the foot-piece' (no year limit) gave 7 hits, all editions of Last's Anatomy. Searches inside the 1972 item (anatomyregionala0000rjla) and the 1984 item (anatomyregionala0000last) returned the full sentence chain. olinside.py places it at leaf n658 of the 1984 edition. The generic phrases ('foot-piece of the stapes', 155 hits; 'perilymph of the vestibule', 244 hits) are stock, but only Last joins 'closed in life by the foot-piece' to 'Inside this window is the perilymph of the vestibule'. Last's next window sentence ('Inside this window is the perilymph of the blind end of the cochlea', for the round window) uses the same formula. Lead check: re-found by inside.py (Last: 7 hits, all editions of Last; Times: the 22 Aug. 1983 issue). Adversarially verified (verify-ow2).

  299. For full paralysis
    of accommodation, three or four drops

    for one or two hours. For the rest of

    25th ed. 1967; 26th ed. 1972 (same wording; later eds. presumably also); homatropine hydrobromide monograph (ophthalmic use) source ↗

    For dilatation of the pupil a 1% solution is usually adequate but for full paralysis of accommodation 3 or 4 drops of a 2% solution may have to be instilled every 15 minutes for 1 to 2 hours.

    The pharmacopoeia's dosage instruction for paralysing the eye's focus, used for refraction tests, is put into a lyric of moonlight and screens. Prynne makes the conditional 'may have to be' into the imperative 'should be', and his added sentence 'For the rest of / your life' changes a one-hour procedure into a permanent condition. Then the speaker can only see through a blur, in which 'accommodation' has also its social sense. The next lines quote Dowland's 'Sight wherein my joys do lie', so the clinical blinding is placed against the lover's sight.

  303. the field is determined
    by the exit window, the lens rim or stop
    which, imaged into image space, subtends
    the smallest angle at the centre.     John Strong, Concepts of Classical Optics The Oval Window (1983) · The Oval Window · l.9906 · p.333 · partial/high

    San Francisco: W. H. Freeman, 1958; ch. XV 'Magnification, Aperture, and Field', p. 345 source ↗

    In this example we take the radii of the rims, hc = hT, for collimator and telescope. The field is determined by the exit window, here Lc' = L'T. The exit window is the lens rim or stop which, imaged into image space, subtends the smallest angle at the center of the exit pupil, here ...

    The textbook definition of an 'exit window', the rim that limits what an optical system can see, is put into the stanza where the hut's opening is named 'in first sight, the oval window'. The window that limits the field of view is defined by the smallest angle, and this matches the poem's narrowing of sight: tunnel vision, the blur spot, glaucoma. Because Prynne stops the sentence at 'the centre', it loses its object (the exit pupil) and appears to refer to the centre of the speaker's vision.

    quotation. Other optics books (Fincham, Heath, Curry) say 'subtends the smallest angle at the centre' of the entrance pupil, but Strong alone has the whole definition. Prynne drops the symbols and stops at 'centre' (British spelling, for Strong's 'center of the exit pupil').

    The clinical sentence comes from a case of poisoning by fruit treated with a molluscicide, and Prynne sets it inside the Fusek lyric of the lonely woman at midnight ('the sweet breath goes about, at midnight / murmuring. The lyric's languor becomes the posture of a poisoned body, and the 'dew-drenched apricot flowers' that follow are shadowed by the treated strawberries.     In Love Restored, Plutus (money) has disguised himself as Love and banned the masque, and the true Love is restored at the end. Jonson's couplet describes the masquers' dance as the motion of the heavens. Prynne attaches it to Fusek's waiting woman ('watches for his return'), so her 'return' becomes a dance step, and puts it before 'Sort and merge', a subroutine. The masque's plot, love usurped by money and then restored, is a small model of the poem's struggle between lyric feeling and the market.

  314. the slant of imperium coming sideways
    "through the competitive examination (chinshih) on Confucian literature." ... They appropriated not the primary
    conditions of labour but their results; ... The denial of feudalism in China
    always leads to political errors, of an
    essentially Trotskyist order:     Stephen P. Dunn, The Fall and Rise of the Asiatic Mode of Production The Oval Window (1983) · The Oval Window · l.9961 · p.336 · partial/high

    London: Routledge & Kegan Paul, 1982; Part Two (the 1931 Leningrad discussion; Godes quoted) and p. 105-6 ('Resurgence'); pages not fully recovered source ↗

    '... could be bought was open to the person who had successfully passed through the competitive examination on Confucian literature.'; '... not the means of production as such but their management; they appropriated not the primary conditions of labor but their results.'; 'It turns out that the denial of feudalism in China, or the theory of it, always leads to political errors, and errors of an essentially Trotskyist order.'

    Dunn's book is a history of the Soviet and Western debate over Marx's 'Asiatic mode of production'. The Trotskyist sentence is his translation of M. Godes at the 1931 Leningrad discussion, where the Asiatic-mode thesis was suppressed as a political heresy. Prynne quotes the Stalinist denunciation flatly and follows it with Wordsworth's 'Calm is all nature as a resting wheel', so the poem's 'Chinese' surface (the Hua-chien chi lyrics) is set beside the Western theory that was used to classify China. The examination and appropriation sentences describe the scholar-official class that the tz'u poets belonged to, which owned 'not the primary conditions of labour but their results'. So the decorative lyrics and the political economy of those who wrote them appear in the same stanza.

    quotation. Not in the criticism corpus or Reeve & Kerridge (1993/1995); but Reeve & Kerridge's The Oval Window: A New Annotated Edition (Bloodaxe, 2018), built from Prynne's source archive, reports sources in optics, anatomy, computer programming and Chinese poetry and was not available to check, so this identification may be recorded there. Lucas Klein (Symposium 70, 2016) says he 'could not find the quotation about imperial exams (jinshi)' in Fusek and asks whether the Marxist rhetoric narrates Chinese Communism; kbgrep 'Asiatic mode', 'Godes', 'Dunn': no source identified.

    Verified: inside.py inside archive.org fallriseofasiati0000dunn: 'passed through the competitive examination on Confucian literature', 'they appropriated not the ... primary conditions of labor but their results' (page break at p. 106), 'denial of feudalism in China, or the theory of it, always leads to political errors, and errors of an essentially Trotskyist order'. Bailey & Llobera, The Asiatic Mode of Production (1981), translate the same Godes passage differently ('seem to have always led to political mistakes, mistakes of precisely a Trotskyist nature'), which confirms that Dunn's wording is Prynne's source. The parenthesis '(chinshih)' was not seen in Dunn's snippet and may be Prynne's insertion.

  319. It is not

    In Lu Ji's preface the sentence states the poet's problem: to understand how good writing works is easier than to write well. Prynne cuts the clause from 'The fact is' and puts it after 'The toy is childish, almost below speech / lip-read by swaying lamps'. A classic of Chinese poetics, which Prynne cited in his 'China Figures' essay in the same year, is thus used against the decorative Chinese material in the poem's late stanzas. It also comments on the poem's own procedure of taking in many kinds of discourse.

    Then THE FOOL, kneeling down, with the swords round his neck, says ... They sing. Then THE FOOL falls down, and the dancers ... sings the following song: Good people all, you see what we have done: / We have cut down our father like the evening sun, / And here he lies all in his purple gore, / And we are afraid he never will dance more.

    The title is the dancers' song: the 'bracelet' is the Lock of interlaced swords set round the Fool's neck before his mock beheading, so the book's title (bands around the throat) is first a folk-play execution. Prynne keeps the play's sequence - the swords on the neck, the fall to the ground, 'we have cut him down, like the evening sun', the fear that 'he never will dance more' - but the Fool's comic resurrection ('That I may rise again and with you have a dance') is cancelled: 'And his dance is gone'. 'Lock-tremors' and 'the next round in the sing-song' carry the play's Lock and its ring of singing dancers into the stock-market idiom of the same stanzas.

    adaptation.

    of green willows     Wei Chuang (836-910), tr. Robin D. S. Yates, The Lament of the Lady of Ch'in Bands Around the Throat (1987) · Marzipan · l.10173 · p.348 · new/high

    in Liu & Lo (eds), Sunflower Splendor: Three Thousand Years of Chinese Poetry (1975), pp. 267 ff.; opening lines source ↗

    a girl like a flower / Resting alone under the shade of the green willows. Her hairpins, shaped like phoenixes, ...

    The pastoral image is the Lady of Ch'in herself, met by the poet on the road outside Ch'ang-an before she tells how the city fell to Huang Ch'ao's rebels in 881. Prynne keeps her pose but cuts her out ('Ah, resting alone'), so the lyric repose is borrowed from a refugee's frame narrative; what follows in 'Marzipan' is her catastrophe, transposed.

  332. Azure banners high in the fragrant
    breeze along the bank ... You see
    as in late spring, shrouded in mist,
    the bright, smooth water.     Wei Chuang (836-910), tr. Lois Fusek, 'River Messages' (Ho ch'uan), Three Lyrics, no. 1 Bands Around the Throat (1987) · Bands Around the Throat: 'Marzipan' · l.10175 · p.348 · new/high

    Lois Fusek (trans.), Among the Flowers: The Hua-chien chi (New York: Columbia University Press, 1982); leaf n258 of the IA scan (the version with syllable counts per line); the Wei Chuang chapter begins p. 66; index 'Sui Embankment, 67, 81, 214' source ↗

    What place can it be, / So shrouded in mists? / In late spring on the Sui Embankment, / The willows grew full and lush green. / The painted oars dripped silken gold. / The azure banners flew high in the fragrant wind. / The water was bright and smooth. / The girls pulling the dragon boats had fine painted brows.

    The Marzipan lifts from Wei Chuang were thought to come from one translation (Yates's 'Lament of the Lady of Ch'in'). Prynne also uses Fusek's version of Wei Chuang's lyric about Emperor Yang of Sui's pleasure-voyage down the Grand Canal: banners, dragon boats and willows on the Sui Embankment. The poet of a dynasty's sack, starving mountain families and a burned corpse is also the poet of imperial luxury, and Prynne cuts between the two. Here 'Azure banners high in the fragrant breeze' is broken off by 'on the ward / floor the fairface was in point / of fact congealed vomit'. Later the 'bright, smooth water' becomes 'eau minerale naturelle / from the hypermarket'. In the Chinese tradition Emperor Yang's canal journey is itself a figure of the ruinous expense that ends a dynasty, which fits the poem's 'Central Production' and 'hypermarket'.

    adaptation. kbgrep 'azure banners' finds only Pietrzak, Levity of Design (2012), who reads the lines as a Romantic pastoral landscape and names no source. Fusek is known as a source of The Oval Window (Li Zhimin, cited by Lucas Klein, Symposium 2016), but not of Marzipan.

    Verified: inside.py inside amongflowershuac0000unse (lending-only; snippets read): 'azure banners', 'shrouded in mists', 'Sui Embankment', 'bright and smooth', 'dragon boats' all occur in this one lyric. olinside.py places 'azure banners flew high' at leaf n258. The lyric is Wei Chuang's 'Ho ch'uan' no. 1 (何處，煙雨，隋堤春暮 ... 翠旗高颭香風，水光融), and the syllable counts that Fusek prints (2,2,4,4,4,6,3,7) match it. Sunflower Splendor has none of these phrases.

    The Lament describes women of the household trapped upstairs as the rebels fire the houses; one hangs dead over the burning beams. Prynne quotes the two lines nearly whole, and reverses the source's 'screams shake the earth' into 'no screams ring' (the Bloodaxe OCR reads 'streams'; the Twose-McCully and Intercapillary Space texts have 'screams'). In a book whose motif is the throat and hanging, the hanging corpse here is a Chinese woman of 881, not a figure of speech.

  335. Nothing more counts but then withers
    for the victor who should, outright,
    Conciliate a broken enemy, or
    destroy them.     Antony Lentin, Lloyd George, Woodrow Wilson and the Guilt of Germany: An Essay in the Pre-History of Appeasement Bands Around the Throat (1987) · Marzipan · l.10199 · p.348 · new/medium

    Leicester University Press, 1984 (repr. Baton Rouge, 1985; also as Guilt at Versailles, Methuen, 1985); conclusion (IA scan page n218) source ↗

    It was a precept of Machiavelli that the victor should either conciliate his enemy or destroy him. The Treaty of Versailles did neither.

    Lentin's sentence is a historian's paraphrase of Machiavelli, used to condemn Versailles, a peace that neither reconciled Germany nor crushed it. In 'Marzipan', between Wei Chuang's sacked capital and Glendower's starving rebellion, the precept about how a victor treats the defeated fits the poem's succession of conquered populations. Prynne's 'Nothing more counts but then withers' sets this realism against the poem's 'Tribute' and 'pledge of election', in the year of an election campaign. Confidence is medium because a paraphrase of a common maxim could be reached independently.

    adaptation. kbgrep 'conciliate', 'Lentin', 'Versailles' (Bands context): nothing relevant. The maxim itself goes back to Machiavelli (Prince ch. 3; Discourses II.23), and Burke's 'you must either conciliate or destroy' circulates, but the combination of 'victor', 'should', 'conciliate', 'enemy', 'destroy' in this order first appears in Lentin. A 1970 novel (Landells, The Royalist Lady) has 'conciliate a broken enemy' verbatim, which shows that the phrasing is natural English.

    Verified: inside.py 'should either conciliate' and 'conciliate his enemy or destroy' (12 hits, none before Lentin 1984; later hits — Purdue, Traynor, Henig, Grieve — quote Lentin); olinside.py gives the page; inside.py on the item for 'Versailles did neither'.

  338. to ask grace
    at a graceless face it is our own
    in the glass of dark recall     Anon., Johnie Armstrong (Child 169) Bands Around the Throat (1987) · Marzipan · l.10211 · p.348 · new/medium

    F. J. Child, The English and Scottish Popular Ballads, vol. 3 (1889), no. 169 C, from Allan Ramsay, The Ever Green (1724); headnote quotes Pitscottie; 169 C st. 22; cf. 169 A st. 11, B st. 13; Mary Hamilton (173) E 13, F 14 source ↗

    'To seik het water beneth cauld yce, / Surely it is a great folie; / I haif asked grace at a graceless face, / But there is nane for my men and me.' [Pitscottie, in Child's headnote:] I am but a fool to seek grace at a graceless face. [Mary Hamilton, at the gallows:] Seek never grace frae a graceless face, / For that ye'll never see.

    The phrase belongs to two Scottish execution ballads: the border reiver Johnie Armstrong, refused pardon by James V and hanged with his men, and Mary Hamilton on the gallows. In 'Marzipan' Prynne turns the plea back on the speaker: the graceless face 'is our own / in the glass'. Because the phrase is proverbial in Scots, the attribution rests on the hanging theme as well as the wording.

  340. and made me eat
    both gravel, dirt and mud, and last
    of all, to gnaw my flesh and blood.     Thomas Phaer, How Owen Glendour, seduced by false prophecies, took upon him to be prince of Wales, and was by Henry, Prince of England, chased to the mountaynes, where hee miserably died for lack of food Bands Around the Throat (1987) · Marzipan · l.10223 · p.348 · new/high

    A Mirror for Magistrates (1559); quoted in John Ruhräh, Pediatrics of the Past (1925), p. 150, J. H. Wylie, The Reign of Henry the Fifth I (1914), and Archaeologia Cambrensis (1846, 1853); standard ed. Lily B. Campbell, The Mirror for Magistrates (Cambridge, 1938); final stanzas source ↗

    The 'me' who ends 'Marzipan' is Owen Glendower, the Welsh rebel prince, speaking as a ghost in the Mirror for Magistrates about his death by starvation in the mountains. Prynne joins him directly to Wei Chuang's starving mountain families, so two rebellions, Chinese and Welsh, end in the same famine. A link to the Chernobyl fallout on Welsh upland pastures is interpretation. Prynne alters 'my dung' to 'to gnaw', which removes the source's grotesque detail and leaves self-consumption.

  341. or in a state localised on an impurity ... stops outflow in mean free time's debate ... on the impurity radius sweeping the lexicon R. J. Elliott and A. F. Gibson, An Introduction to Solid State Physics and its Applications Bands Around the Throat (1987) · Punishment Routines · l.10248 · p.350 · new/high

    London: Macmillan, 1974; impurity-state section (IA scan n516); glossary of symbols ('impurity radius a_I'); s. 2.7 'Mean free time and mean free path' source ↗

    For a state localised on an impurity the energy depends on the local atomic displacements. ... [glossary:] exciton radius ... impurity radius ... [s. 2.7:] Mean free time and mean free path ... The average time is called the mean free time t.

    Three terms in two stanzas come from one standard semiconductor textbook: the electron state localised on an impurity atom, the impurity radius, and the mean free time between collisions. In doping, a planned impurity changes what a crystal conducts; Prynne applies this to the 'necklace' that 'plugs the blocked echo current' and to the word 'padlocked by voiceprint'. The physics gives literal sense to Perril's phrase 'planned impurity': the voice is governed by what is deliberately put into it.

  342. At the neckline the word you give then
    is padlocked by voiceprint ... It must be the clasp of waiting hands     John Milton, Colasterion (1645); Of Reformation (1641) Bands Around the Throat (1987) · Punishment Routines · l.10254 · p.350 · partial/low

    Prose Works, ed. J. A. St John (Bohn, 1848), vols 2-3; Colasterion, reply to the fourth argument; Of Reformation, Book II, closing prayer source ↗

    [Colasterion] Let not therefore, under the name of fulfilling charity, such an unmerciful and more than legal yoke be padlocked upon the neck of any Christian. ... [Of Reformation] in supereminence of beatific vision, progressing the dateless and irrevoluble circle of eternity, shall clasp inseparable hands with joy and bliss, in overmeasure for ever.

    In Colasterion Milton argues for divorce, and the padlock is the legal yoke of an unwanted marriage fixed 'upon the neck'. Prynne moves it to the 'neckline', where it locks the given word (a vow or pledge) 'by voiceprint'. The 'clasp of waiting hands' recalls the saints of Milton's closing prayer in Of Reformation, who 'clasp inseparable hands' in eternity, in contrast to the prelates thrown down into hell. In the poem, this clasp only waits by 'the waiting wall of money'. These two words support King's claim with specific evidence. They do not show that Prynne recombines whole sentences, so the borrowing is better called a lexical allusion.

    allusion. King (Jacket2, 2021, n. 64) names both Milton tracts (mislabelling Of Reformation) and cites a Prynne holograph source list (Prynne Papers, folder 1601).

    Verified: Downloaded the Bohn Prose Works vols 2 and 3 (djvu text), cut out Of Reformation and Colasterion, and compared the poem's vocabulary with both. 'padlocked' occurs once in Colasterion, as a yoke padlocked on the neck; 'clasp ... hands' occurs in the last sentence of Of Reformation. No longer verbatim run exists.

The voluntary 'common pool' of the welfare state is set against a privatised economy of blood, in a poem whose title is a phrase for good health.

  348. as the bills mount in the pre-tax void,
    all our bills grinding by the dream of friendship ... undone by goodness not waiting     William Shakespeare, Timon of Athens Bands Around the Throat (1987) · Almost Lunch-Time · l.10365 · p.354 · new/high

    any standard text (checked against Project Gutenberg #1536); III.iv (Philotus: 'All our bills.'); IV.ii.33-38 (Flavius) source ↗

    TITUS. My lord, here is my bill. LUCIUS. Here's mine. HORTENSIUS. And mine, my lord. BOTH VARRO'S SERVANTS. And ours, my lord. PHILOTUS. All our bills. TIMON. Knock me down with 'em! Cleave me to the girdle. ... [IV.ii] Who would be so mocked with glory, or to live / But in a dream of friendship, / To have his pomp and all what state compounds / But only painted, like his varnished friends? / Poor honest lord, brought low by his own heart, / Undone by goodness! Strange, unusual blood / When man's worst sin is he does too much good!

    Three phrases come from the two scenes of Timon's ruin: the creditors' servants pressing their bills at his door, and his steward's lament for a lord destroyed by his own generosity and his false friends. In a poem of menus, pre-tax voids and standing orders, Timon makes the debt literal: the 'dream of friendship' is the credit that the bills grind down. 'Undone by goodness' then sharpens 'Stupidly good / as a standing order' (Milton's Satan, found by the first pass): goodness is the condition of being ruined, whether through Satan's moment of abstraction or Timon's bounty.

  349. in double running, cloud filling. embroidery terms of art, 'cloud filling' (stitch) Bands Around the Throat (1987) · Almost Lunch-Time · l.10367 · p.354 · new/medium

    e.g. Butler, Batsford Encyclopaedia of Embroidery Stitches (1968/1979); Edith John, Filling Stitches (1967); stitch index ('Cloud filling 287'; 'Double running', 'Interlaced double running') source ↗

    Double running ... Interlaced double running ... Cloud filling ... Maltese cross ... Laced lattice filling

    Two adjacent embroidery stitch names: double running (Holbein stitch, which is identical on both faces of the cloth) and cloud filling (an open lattice laced through foundation stitches). Placed after 'all our bills grinding', they read as financial terms (double-entry, double running costs, a filled cloud of credit). The needlework sense makes the double dealing into a pattern that looks the same from either side. This is a vocabulary echo from a technical register, not a quotation from a particular manual.

    echo. kbgrep 'double running', 'cloud filling': no hits.

    Verified: inside.py 'cloud filling' and 'double running' (both terms of art in embroidery manuals: Edith John, Filling Stitches, 1967; Hobbs, Crewel Embroidery Primer, 1973); both occur in Butler's encyclopaedia (inside.py with identifier).

  354. by the fanning plumes above her brow Percy Bysshe Shelley, Prometheus Unbound Bands Around the Throat (1987) · Ein Heldenleben · l.10398 · p.355 · new/high

    1820; checked against Project Gutenberg #4797 (Complete Poetical Works); Act I, ll. 749-777 (Fourth Spirit, Ione, Sixth Spirit) source ↗

    Forms more real than living man, / Nurslings of immortality! ... IONE: Behold'st thou not two shapes from the east and west / Come, as two doves to one beloved nest, / Twin nurslings of the all-sustaining air / On swift still wings glide down the atmosphere? ... SIXTH SPIRIT: Ah, sister! Desolation is a delicate thing: / It walks not on the earth, it floats not on the air, / But treads with lulling footstep, and fans with silent wing / The tender hopes which in their hearts the best and gentlest bear; / Who, soothed to false repose by the fanning plumes above / And the music-stirring motion of its soft and busy feet, / Dream visions of aereal joy, and call the monster, Love, / And wake, and find the shadow Pain, as he whom now we greet.

    'The fanning plumes above' is verbatim from the Sixth Spirit's song, and 'nurseling' and 'glide' come from the lines just before it, in the same sequence of comforting spirits sent to Prometheus. Shelley's Desolation fans hope with its plumes until hope is 'soothed to false repose' and wakes to Pain; Prynne puts the plumes on a woman's brow as she walks to the lime-pits, so that the consolation is a funeral head-dress. Shelley's 'nurslings of immortality', the poet's forms 'more real than living man', become 'the very nurseling of first care', which belongs to a poem that speaks of 'comforting words' and 'a done thing'. Under the title Ein Heldenleben, Shelley's Titan-hero gives the borrowed lyricism its romantic stake.

Lloyd's book also prints the mining song that poem 4 quotes, so a single anthology, Lloyd's Marxist history of English folk song, supplies at least two of the work songs that Wilkinson heard in the sequence.     'O man, for thy sake' is Christ speaking from the cross in the Passion lyric 'Woefully arrayed'. Cornysh's setting makes this phrase the climax of the song, and Stevens's study of early Tudor song draws attention to it. Prynne puts the phrase between the shanty's 'Walk him along' and 'carry him ... over to the burying ground'. The work-song burial of General Taylor therefore becomes a deposition from the cross, which is the reading that Wilkinson reached by way of Joseph of Arimathea. The lyric's catalogue of a beaten, nailed and tugged body ('thus bobbid', 'the sturdy nailis', 'a spere my hert dyd race') also stands behind the sequence's blows and the 'metal spike' of the last poem. It is a sung lyric of torture addressed to the bystander who is responsible, which suits a sequence about bodies made to 'sing out'.

    In the legend, book and sword fall from heaven tied together. Obedience to the written law saves Israel from the sword. Prynne keeps the first clause verbatim but reverses the preposition: 'delivered from' becomes 'delivered to'. The choice is now compliance or execution, not deliverance. The poem opens 'it is compliance ... as with one voice'. Word Order was written in the year of Tiananmen, which suggests that the line makes the scriptural promise of safety through the book into the logic of a state that enforces its text with the sword.

Amiens' 'Blow, blow' (Wilkinson) sits next to the nursery rhyme's 'doth blow ... we shall have snow', which Prynne cuts down to its second line after 'Cold and blow dry'. It adds the lullaby to the sequence's catalogue of work songs, drinking songs and shanties.

  370. fire down below traditional (capstan shanty), Fire Down Below Word Order (1989) · Word Order, 17 ('Cold and blow dry as') · l.10731 · p.376 · new/low

    e.g. Michael Hurd, Sailors' Songs and Shanties (1965); James Reeves, The Merry-Go-Round (1957); refrain source ↗

    Fire in the galley, fire down below; / It's fetch a bucket of water, boys, / There's fire down below.

    Wilkinson argues that the shanty is the formal key of Word Order. A third shanty title stands here as a line by itself, between 'invasive, ground cover' and 'vinca alkaloids'. The chain runs from periwinkle (Vinca) as an invasive ground plant, to the anti-cancer vinca drugs, to an internal burning. So the shanty's alarm about fire below decks is turned towards the body and its chemotherapy, in a poem that also puns 'Pinkepinke invincible' on vinca. 'Fire down below' is common (3,540 IA hits before 1990), so it is the shanty title in a shanty-filled sequence, not a verified quotation.

  371. Truthfulness-by-silence is truthfulness, and expectation thereof is expectation of truthfulness; but expectation of truthfulness-by-silence is not yet trust. David Lewis David Lewis, 'Languages and Language', in Keith Gunderson (ed.), Language, Mind, and Knowledge (Minnesota Studies in the Philosophy of Science VII) Not-You (1993) · Not-You (epigraph) · l.10772 · p.383 · acknowledged/high

    Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press, 1975; reprinted in Lewis, Philosophical Papers I (1983), and Martinich, The Philosophy of Language (1985); pp. 3-35 (section on truthfulness and trust; near IA leaf n442) source ↗

    ... expectation of truthfulness; but expectation of truthfulness-by-silence is not yet trust. Expectation of (successful) truthfulness ...

    In Lewis's paper, a population uses a language by a convention of truthfulness and trust. One way to stay truthful with the 'garbage' sentences is never to utter them, which he calls truthfulness-by-silence. Expecting someone to keep silent is not yet trusting what they say. The epigraph frames a book whose syntax withholds assertion, and it warns the reader that expecting such silence is not yet trust.

    quotation. Epigraph signed 'David Lewis'. M. A. King (Jacket2, 2021) mentions the Lewis epigraph but gives no source text. The source is not identified in the kb.

    Verified: inside.py 'expectation of truthfulness-by-silence': Lewis 1975 and reprints (Martinich, Philosophy of Language 1985; Readings in Language and Mind 1996).

  372. Love of semiconductors is not enough. Thomas Nagel Thomas Nagel, Equality and Partiality Not-You (1993) · Not-You (epigraph) · l.10777 · p.383 · acknowledged/high

    New York and Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991; IA leaf n218 (chapter on equality and economic motivation) source ↗

    ...them what exactly to make in their semiconductor plant. Benevolence is not enough. Even love of semiconductors is not enough. Among those who have to think of new things to ...

    Nagel argues that people who must invent and manage a semiconductor plant cannot be moved by benevolence or by love of the product. They need incentives, which is why the egalitarian ideal is utopian. Prynne cuts away 'Benevolence is not enough' and 'Even'. What is left reads like an epitaph for love in a technological economy. The next entry shows that Prynne went on drawing on the same book.

  374. The cure is won across twice ... what to shun of this set cure's topmost
    retort     Nahum Tate (words), Henry Purcell (music), Dido and Aeneas Not-You (1993) · Not-You ('The cure is won across twice', p. 390) · l.10865 · p.390 · new/high

    Great minds against themselves conspire, / And shun the cure they most desire.

    Tate's couplet is the chorus's verdict on Dido sending Aeneas away: the remedy she wants is the one she refuses. Prynne's poem opens with the cure 'won' and ends by asking 'what to shun of this set cure', and the centre poem repeats it as 'to shun this terrible cure' (line 10962). The borrowed paradox of self-defeating desire runs through the book's medical and sales language ('cure', 'bidder', 'retort'). The cure of the earlier choruses ('she that wounds can only cure the smart', Act I) stands behind it too. The same libretto supplies at least a dozen further phrases across pp. 388-407 (see the other entries), so the source is fixed by corroboration, not by one string. A third instance, 'to shun this terrible cure' (l. 10962), is the closest of the three to Tate.

  376. staring ahead to the empty room where
    brightness is born and tagged     Chuang Tzu, tr. Burton Watson, The Complete Works of Chuang Tzu, ch. 4 'In the World of Men' Not-You (1993) · Not-You ('The cure is won across twice') · l.10868 · p.390 · new/high

    New York: Columbia University Press, 1968; p. 58 (the 'fasting of the mind'; index: 'Sitting but racing around, 58') source ↗

    Look into that closed room, the empty chamber where brightness is born! Fortune and blessing gather where there is stillness. But if you do not keep still - this is what is called sitting but racing around.

    Zhuangzi's empty chamber is the emptied mind of the 'fasting of the mind'. In stillness, brightness is born and fortune gathers. Prynne puts the phrase in a saleroom. 'Glitter patches so cheap they thrill each bidder' face it, the bidders 'stare ahead' instead of sitting still, and the brightness is 'born and tagged', given a price at birth. The poem stages exactly what the passage forbids: 'sitting but racing around'. The Taoist cure ('the cure is won', 'this set cure') is turned into the consumer cure that the book calls 'this terrible cure'.

    'Remember me', set off by colons as a quotation, is the refrain of the most famous English aria. Its context is fixed by the other Dido phrases on the page. 'Give now over' bends the Prologue's 'Now carry your game, or forever give o're', the shepherds' advice to woo or give up. So the poem ends with the abandoned queen's request and a pastoral instruction to quit. Prynne reverses the opera's order, where the shepherds' cheerful 'give o're' comes long before the lament. The same libretto supplies at least a dozen further phrases across pp. 388-407 (see the other entries), so the source is fixed by corroboration, not by one string. 'Remember me' alone is ubiquitous (Hamlet's ghost is the competing famous source); the Dido context of the page decides it. 'Give now over' < 'give o're' (Prologue) is tentative only.

    libretto printed 1689 ('An Opera Perform'd at Mr. Josias Priest's Boarding-School at Chelsey'); ed. Curtis Price, Dido and Aeneas: An Opera (Norton Critical Score, New York: Norton, 1986), which prints the 1689 libretto with Prologue and Epilogue; Prologue, Phoebus's opening lines source ↗

    From Aurora's spicy bed, / Phoebus rears his sacred head. / His coursers advancing, / Curvetting and prancing

    The 1689 libretto opens with the sun rising 'from Aurora's spicy bed'. Prynne's centre poem opens the same way, but the rising thing is 'a rising vertical trust', a financial and corporate entity, not Phoebus. The later lines of the same poem take more of the Prologue ('outshining', 'blind', 'gentle planets', 'the day advances'). So the centre poem is built on the opera's lost prologue, whose music does not survive. An overlay of the phoenix topos ('gather as others have', spices gathered for a rebirth) is possible but not needed. The same libretto supplies at least a dozen further phrases across pp. 388-407 (see the other entries), so the source is fixed by corroboration, not by one string. 'Spicy bed' is a stock Augustan phrase; the attribution rests on the Prologue sequence that follows in this poem.

  380. to claim plus set-off ... in pro tanto extinction legal terminology (set-off; 'pro tanto' extinction of a debt), no single text Not-You (1993) · Not-You ('With an eye turning for entry') · l.10961 · p.394 · new/low

    on compensation (set-off) source ↗

    ...parties are sustained, the one will be set in pro tanto extinction of the other, and decree given to the pursuer ...

    'Pro tanto extinction' is the legal term for a debt extinguished 'to that extent' by a counter-claim, which is exactly what set-off does. Prynne puts the two terms close together in the same poem. That suggests the doctrine and not only its vocabulary. Its next word is 'Blind', and the doctrine becomes an image of lives cancelled against each other in an account.

  385. there
    is no default position at true discount     Thomas Nagel, Equality and Partiality Not-You (1993) · Not-You ('With an eye turning for entry', the centre poem) · l.10976 · p.394 · new/high

    New York and Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991; discussion of the distribution of benefits under a market system source ↗

    ...regarded as having chosen to permit the distribution of benefits on morally irrelevant grounds. There is no default position that doesn't have to be justified because it is not chosen. Any way in which the ...

    Nagel argues that a society cannot treat the distribution of goods produced by the market as a neutral starting point that needs no justification. Leaving things alone is also a choice. The phrase occurs in the long centre poem of Not-You, among 'claim plus set-off', 'provably liquid', 'pro tanto extinction' and 'a price floor'. 'At true discount' mixes Nagel's point into banking language, so a moral claim that there is no innocent baseline becomes a pricing term. With the epigraph it shows that Prynne read Equality and Partiality closely and took more from it than he acknowledged.
