  389. as then: Abend ist im alten Garten geworden. Georg Trakl, Nachlass, Fragment 4, 'Im Frühling' Not-You (1993) · Not-You ('Lights go forward to flight assessment checks') · l.11072 · p.401 · new/high

    Dichtungen und Briefe, ed. Walther Killy and Hans Szklenar (Salzburg: Otto Müller, 1969), historisch-kritische Ausgabe vol. 1; vol. 1, p. 429 (one-volume edition 1970, c. p. 236) source ↗

    Fragment 4 IM FRÜHLING Abend ist im alten Garten geworden.

    The poem's Gulf War vocabulary ('flight assessment checks', 'incessant false alerts at re-entry', 'diagnose and record', 'front-line') ends on an entire Trakl poem. It is an unfinished one-line fragment, 'In Spring': evening has come in the old garden. 'As then' points back to Trakl's own war, in which he died in 1914 after serving as a medical orderly at Grodek. So the line sets a poet broken by the casualties of the first technological war against the 'dainty devices' of the 1991 one. The fragment is complete and incomplete at once, and that suits a book about statements that do not reach the reader ('Not-You').

    quotation. kbgrep 'alten Garten', 'Abend ist': no hits. Trakl is known as an interest of Prynne (his 1960s Cambridge Review notice, cited by Clark, Jacket 24). Web search 'Abend ist im alten Garten geworden Prynne': nothing.

  395. To say
    so only: she, she, she, and only she: then nearly back.     John Dowland (lyricist anonymous), 'Say, Love, if ever thou didst find', The Third and Last Book of Songs or Airs Her Weasels Wild Returning (1994) · Then So Much She Did (Her Weasels Wild Returning) · l.11241 · p.412 · new/high

    A. H. Bullen (ed.), Lyrics from the Song-Books of the Elizabethan Age (1887; archive.org copy dated 1897); Fellowes, English Madrigal Verse (1920), p. 482; Bullen, More Lyrics (1888); Bullen, p. 127 (Love-Poems) source ↗

    'Say, Love, if ever thou didst find / A woman with a constant mind.' 'None but one.' 'And what should that rare mirror be?' 'Some goddess or some queen is She.' / She, She, She, and only She, / She only queen of love and beauty. ... 'See the moon / That ever in one change doth grow / Yet still the same: and, She is so.' / So, so, so, and only So! ... There is no queen of love but She.' / She, She, She, and only She, / She only queen of love and beauty.

    The line that critics have taken as the sequence's signature obsession is a refrain from an Elizabethan lute-song in praise of the one woman 'with a constant mind', a queen 'not subject to Love's bow' (often read as Elizabeth). Prynne keeps the song's frame: Dowland's text is a dialogue begun by 'Say, Love', and its third stanza turns the refrain on 'So, so, so, and only So'; Prynne's 'To say / so only:' compresses both before he gives the 'she' refrain. The song's constancy-in-change ('See the moon / That ever in one change doth grow / Yet still the same') fits a poem of 'fade still branching', 'mutation' and 'then back'. The courtly cult of the unattainable, singular woman is set against 'mind lesions finely displayed' and an 'override by the park signal'.

Web search: nothing.

  396. Go with us, and all
    the haunt be ours to the premium ground turn allowed.     William Shakespeare, Antony and Cleopatra Her Weasels Wild Returning (1994) · Attending Her Aggregate, Detour (Her Weasels Wild Returning) · l.11268 · p.413 · new/high

    any standard text; IV.xiv.50-54 source ↗

    Eros!—I come, my queen.—Eros!—Stay for me. / Where souls do couch on flowers, we'll hand in hand, / And with our sprightly port make the ghosts gaze. / Dido and her Aeneas shall want troops, / And all the haunt be ours.

    Antony speaks the line as he resolves to fall on his sword and join Cleopatra, whom he believes dead, among the shades; the 'haunt' is the underworld meadow the lovers will take over. Prynne's 'Go with us' turns Antony's solitary suicide into an invitation, and 'premium ground' makes the Elysian haunt a piece of real estate. The poem's 'Abandon, abundant' and 'don't take on so' sit just before the line, so the lift brings a love-death into the sequence's feminine 'Really hers'.

  397. time after time found; the little pieces of the whole body
    invented as lucid driftwork     Eudora Welty, Delta Wedding Her Weasels Wild Returning (1994) · Well Enough in Her Killing Alter (Her Weasels Wild Returning) · l.11279 · p.414 · new/high

    New York: Harcourt, Brace, 1946 (Prynne's Caius reading list gives Harcourt Brace / Virago, 1982); Robbie Reid's thoughts on the Fairchild women (p. 146 in the edition cited by Hoffman 1967) source ↗

    those women knew what to ask of their men. Adoration, first—but least. Then, small sacrifice by small sacrifice, the little pieces of the whole body! Robbie, with the sun on her head, could scream to see the thousand little ...

    In Welty, Robbie, who has married into the Fairchild family, sees the family's women claim their men first with adoration and then, 'small sacrifice by small sacrifice', piece by piece of the body. Prynne lifts the seven-word phrase whole. The lift is one of four from Delta Wedding in this poem. It brings Robbie's possessive, embattled love for George into a poem about consent ('We'll consent'), recovery ('to recoup') and a body that is 'invented'. Welty's piecemeal sacrifice becomes 'time after time found' and 'driftwork', which keeps the sense of a body given up in fragments.

Taken alone, three words would be weak evidence, but the phrase sits two lines after the verbatim 'little pieces of the whole body' from the same Robbie chapter, and Welty critics quote it as a key phrase. 'Freehand' makes Welty's real body a sketch drawn without a guide, in the same way as the 'invented ... driftwork' just before it.

Prynne keeps the threat of the impending light and makes it the edge of exposure: 'no safe / place'. The four-word lift is the second from Delta Wedding in three lines, which supports the attribution.

    ... includes the cudgel. (c) Why should the dog ever be displeased spontaneously? Leibniz distinguishes the spontaneous from ...

    The epigraph is not Leibniz's own sentence but a question in Austin Farrer's introduction, glossing Leibniz's example of the dog beaten while it eats: Farrer asks why pain should ever arise 'spontaneously' from within a monad whose states unfold from its own nature. Prynne's citation is exact ('intro. by Austin Farrer'), so the sequence opens on a modern philosopher's paraphrase of the problem of evil in monadology, not on the Theodicy itself. That fits a book whose method (Korsh, Kemp Smith's Kant, Bailey & Murray) works through translations, textbooks and secondary expositions rather than primary sources.

    quotation. Prynne cites the volume ('intro. by Austin Farrer (1951)'). Criticism treats the epigraph as Leibniz's; kbgrep 'displeased spontaneously' gives no hits, so the point that the sentence is Farrer's, not Leibniz's, appears unrecorded.

    The Kant lift is longer than the two recorded phrases. Prynne takes one continuous run of A141-143, the monogram sentence and the schema of reality, and puts Korsh's control-flow tokens ('if (set if true)', 'goto', 'if else', '> zero', 'count to null') between Kant's words. Kant's degree of sensation, which descends 'to its cessation in nothingness (= 0)', becomes a loop counter decremented to null. The monogram of pure imagination is written out as program code, and the schematism, Kant's 'art concealed in the depths of the human soul', becomes an algorithm.

    Every line of Whitman's poem is taken apart in order: 'silver stars fading', 'Milky', 'weft of white detaching', 'Coals', 'thirty-eight', 'baleful and burning', 'Scarlet, significant, hands off warning', 'henceforth flaunt from these shores'; even 'World take good notice' survives as 'world animation' and 'notation'. Whitman's poem is a warning to the world from the Union flag, its stars and stripes read as fire and blood. Prynne splices it with the breast-implant manual ('cut ... position and peel back') and Reich's 'Come Out' ('out to show'), so the flag of a nation at war becomes skin flayed for display and 'hands off warning' becomes a surgical or commercial disclaimer. The thirty-eight coals of the flag stand behind the poem's 'thirty-eight'. Whitman's 'weft of white detaching' is also a better source than eye-dissection literature for 'to show weft of' (7.8), which Goddard (2017) assigned to the latter. Prynne's Caius reading list on Whitman includes Drum-Taps.

Middleton's and Goddard's readings of the poem (Reich, eye dissection, the implant manual) do not cite Whitman. Prynne's own Whitman and Truth (2022) shows long attention to Whitman's war writing. Goddard (2017) assigns 'to show weft of' to eye-dissection literature; Whitman is not named.

[I.1.5] through you the state suffers no loss, either from violence or from fraud. [Calvin:] Hence arose the proverb, Crowdy and rowdy [Varro in Aul. Gell. 13.11.3]. ... For as a mirror displays a man's face to himself ... [FACE:] Synesius: the face of a captured city. Cicero: And yet we have lost the face of the city.

    De Clementia opens as a mirror for a prince: Nero sees his clemency reflected while he looks down on the rioting mob, and the state suffers no loss 'from violence or from fraud'. Calvin glosses the mob with Varro's 'Crowdy and rowdy'. Prynne turns these words round ('Bored with fraud rowdy crowds') and puts them in a shopping mall: the mirror becomes the shop-fitter's 'mirror facings', the 'face of the city' that Cicero says was lost becomes 'losing face ... in face of / the city'. The prince's mirror of virtue becomes the 'cheat show' of commercial display. This continues the Calvin/Seneca material that the first pass found in the previous poem ('face of a captured city', 'bare outline of captured cities').

    echo.

    Garden Rue ... the leaves ... be divided into wings ... of a gray colour or greenish blew: the floures in the top of the branches are of a pale yellow consisting of foure little leaves, something hollow: in the middle of which standeth up a little head or button foure square, seldome five square, containing as many little coffers as it hath corners, being compassed about with divers little yellow threds ... the seed groweth in the little coffers ... The herb a little boiled or skalded ... quickens the sight. The same applied with hony and the juice of Fennell, is a remedie against dim eies. ... [wild Rue] fumeth out a vapor or aire so hurtfull that it scorches the face of him that looketh upon it, raising up blisters ... when the Weesell is to fight with the serpent, shee armeth her selfe by eating Rue.

    'Herb of grace' is rue, and the poem's last clause quotes Gerard's description of the rue flower verbatim: 'a little head or button'. With that source the vision lexicon of the final poem becomes clear. Gerard's rue 'quickens the sight' and, with fennel, cures 'dim eies' (compare 'In the dim / gray light', 'silver fennel', 'the ocular lens'). Its leaves are 'gray' and 'divided into wings' ('under wing'). Its yellow flowers have 'little yellow threds' round packed 'little coffers' of seed ('tonic / yellow signal; the arrays lie packed'; 'force their seed'). Wild rue 'scorches the face ... raising up blisters' ('all / brows raised'). Calvin's 'defect of strictness' (pity) is thus attached to the herb of grace and ruth. Gerard's weasel that 'armeth her selfe by eating Rue' also recalls the title of the previous collection, Her Weasels Wild Returning (1994).

    quotation.

    Mattheck & Breloer, The Body Language of Trees (HMSO, 1994), the book Prynne gave to Peter Larkin; Wood (Springer, 1997) and Design in Nature (1998) as evidence of usage; Wood, IA scan leaf n150 (Fig. 110-111, 'hazard beam' failure); Design in Nature, chapters 'The Hazard Beam: Fatal Failure or Last Resort?' (p. 147) and 'Windthrow' (p. 159) source ↗

    Spruce trees mostly fail due to windthrow or through hazard beam cleavage (Fig. 110). ... illustrates the failure principle of the hazard beam. Hazard beam failure is the reversal of tree failure ... (Wood); 'Wind-throw (Fig. 125) also occurs relatively frequently'; 'Fig. 125. Windthrow with root plate lifted out' (Design in Nature)

    'Hazard beam' is Mattheck's coinage for a curved bough or stem that splits lengthwise under load, and 'windthrow' is the other way a tree fails, with the root plate torn out; Mattheck puts the two in one sentence and Prynne puts them two lines apart. The arboricultural vocabulary of visual tree assessment then runs through the poem: 'Rip brace', 'root planed' (perhaps root plate), 'Its bark declining splits up', 'thin severance' (the severance cut of pruning), 'down bracket' and 'grappled fruiting body' (the fungal signs of decay at the stem base), 'agaric'. Mattheck reads a tree's form as 'body language' that predicts its failure; Red D Gypsum, under its epigraph on the asymmetric volatility smile, sets that forensic reading of structural risk beside the derivative trader's; a double sense of 'hazard' lights in 'yellow lights' is the reader's gloss.

    adaptation. kbgrep 'hazard beam', 'windthrow', 'wind throw': no hits in Prynne criticism. kbgrep 'Mattheck' finds only a Tears in the Fence review of Peter Larkin's Encroach to Resume, which says The Body Language of Trees was 'a book given to Larkin by J H Prynne'. So Prynne owned and circulated the book, but its use in Red D Gypsum is not recorded.

    Verified: inside.py 'hazard beam' (before 1999: 17 hits; no year: 35) returns only Mattheck's two Springer books and laser/car-switch noise before 1999; item searches of woodinternalopti0000matt and designinnaturele0000matt show 'hazard beam' and 'windthrow' in the same sentence and chapter run. The Body Language of Trees is not on IA; its use of the term is attested by Lonsdale, Principles of Tree Hazard Assessment (1999: 'The "hazard beam" Mattheck and Breloer [106] have drawn attention') and by catalogue descriptions.

    Andrew Wilton with Rosalind Mallord Turner, London: Tate Gallery, 1990; transcription of a Verse Book draft, IA leaf n194 source ↗

    [OCR of Wilton's diplomatic transcription, deletions and interlineations run together:] "... the cheek blush ... And then one stealing tear / Making to the ... sight / Of blushing Concerns startin[g] / Loves mellow blush reflected / Kiss one gay light ask the / 'Then show to ho[pe] the lost natures sweet ... her finest charm heal the even Natures tear on the blush cheek who the vital our love betrays ... bright and oft ... every age / By thy own smile blush shining ... again / doubt yet believing hope soft yielding light in the heart glows"; on the same draft: "... wound ... Then nature enquires / To the gay accent Request ..."

    The opening lyric is a re-lineation of one of Turner's half-legible draft love-songs, kept with its deletions, false starts and broken syntax ('Making to the ... sight / Of blushing Concerns startin'). Prynne does not parody a finished poem. He sets out the painter's failed attempt at verse, so the stanza's odd grammar ('making to the one', 'request the lost') is Turner's own unrevised draft. This changes the 'blush' from a moral or erotic sign (Nolan's Hester) to a painter's colour-word ('Loves mellow blush reflected', 'blush shining'), a tint of light on a surface, which agrees with the title's Tempest 'sea-change' and with the gossamer-in-slant-sun epigraph. It also makes the book start in amateur Romantic song-writing, which the later stanzas continue with Byron's 'Stanzas for Music', broadside ballads and nursery songs.

    adaptation. kbgrep 'stealing tear', 'blush shining', 'doubt yet believing' find only Nolan, 'Capital Calves' (Jacket 24, 2003), who quotes the stanza and reads it via Hester Prynne's blush in The Scarlet Letter; no Turner source is noted. kbgrep 'Verse Book' finds Wilton's book on Prynne's own Caius reading list for the Romantic period ('Wilton (Andrew), Painting and Poetry; Turner's 'Verse Book' and his Work of ...'), which shows that Prynne knew it. A web search for Prynne + 'Pearls That Were' + Turner 'Verse Book' gives nothing.

    her charms gash inflected exile's boast for
    breakfast onwards ... Pandora, accomplice of her
    fiery arm alight with mock fury ... flash out at oddity.     Samuel Johnson, Irene: A Tragedy Triodes (1999) · Triodes, Book I [p. 486, 'Unlocking her oven with a zip'] · l.12362 · p.486 · new/high

    probably Fleeman, The Complete English Poems (Penguin, 1971); II.vii (Mahomet: 'Thus bright in tears'); III.ix (Aspasia: 'When I am gone, remember'); V.iv (Abdalla: 'Shall plume her charms'; Demetrius: 'the frantick boast'); V.v (Aspasia to Irene: 'illustrious exile'); V.xii (Mahomet: 'the curs'd accomplice of her treason'); III.i (Abdalla: 'Flash out at once') source ↗

    Ah! cease, Irene, cease those flowing sorrows ... How will the matchless beauties of Irene, / Thus bright in tears, thus amiable in ruin ... Adorn a throne (II.vii) | When I am gone, remember, O! remember, / That none are great, or happy, but the virtuous. (III.ix) | Henceforth shall live for me; for me alone / Shall plume her charms, and, with attentive watch, / Steal from Abdalla's eye the sign to smile. ... Advance, and perish in the frantick boast. (V.iv) | Companion of our flight, illustrious exile (V.v) | And thou, the curs'd accomplice of her treason (V.xii) | The subtler flames, emitted from the sky, / Flash out at once, with strength above resistance. (III.i)

    The Irene of Triodes is Johnson's Irene: the Greek captive in Constantinople in 1453 who gives up her faith for Mahomet's offer of a throne and is strangled by his mutes. Prynne makes a cento of the play's wooing and betrayal speeches; the secure core is the sultan's 'thus bright in tears', Aspasia's farewell 'when I am gone, remember', and Abdalla's 'shall plume her charms' ('exile's boast', 'accomplice of her' and 'flash out at' are probable members only) and recasts them as tariff talk ('second billing', 'talktime', 'cash advance'). The play's subject is the sale of a self, conscience against 'love and empire', and this gives the sequence its ethical plot. Irene's name means 'peace' in Greek, so Book III's 'Irene, we are the slave market now' and the decommissioning language of p. 513 take place under the sign of a peace already sold.

    adaptation. kbgrep 'plume her charms', 'starry lamps', 'Johnson's Irene': no hits. Critics (Nolan, Shepard, Potts, Sankar) treat Irene and Pandora as 'archetypal' or emblematic figures; none names Johnson's play. Web search 'Triodes' Prynne Irene Johnson: nothing. Prynne's Caius reading list for Johnson cites the Smith/McAdam and Fleeman editions, which both print Irene. Purves, 'J.H. Prynne's Triodes' (The Paper 7, 2003) could not be checked.

    Verified: Exhaustive n-gram comparison of Triodes against the Project Gutenberg text of Johnson's Works (PG 10835, Irene at its ll. 4750-8166). One 17-line poem holds five runs from five scenes of the play, in the play's own order of speakers' wording: 'thus bright in [tears]', 'when I am gone[,] remember', 'shall plume her charms', 'accomplice of her', 'flash out at'.

    London: Allen Lane The Penguin Press, 1999 (Penguin Classics); 'Bilgames and the Netherworld' (Sumerian), ll. 7-9, 18 (p. 179) and ll. 156-7 (p. 183) source ↗

    after bread had been swallowed in the sanctuaries of the land, / after the ovens of the land had been fired up with bellows, / after heaven had been parted from earth, / after earth had been separated from heaven, ... the big ones were hailstones that made the reeds jump ... The son who had a mother, she brought him bread, / the brother who had a sister, she poured him water.

    The opening formula of the Sumerian poem tells of the cosmogonic moment ('after earth had been separated from heaven') before the huluppu-tree and the netherworld episodes. Prynne bends George's 'fired up with bellows' into 'the bellows of stupid amazement' and moves the hailstones that 'made the reeds jump' to the parting of earth and sky. In the couplet of the mothers and sisters who feed the young men exhausted by Bilgames's ball game, he replaces 'poured him water' with a second 'brought him bread', and so the providing women are flattened into 'abundance of necessity'. In the source the next event is the widows' outcry that sends the toys into the underworld. In 1999 Prynne wrote to George that the epic's lesson is 'George's 'vanity of the hero's quest' (Introduction, p. xxxvi)'.

    adaptation. Prynne's 'Letter to Dr Andrew George, c/o Penguin Books' (dated 1 Aug. 1999; Quid 5, 2000) records that he read this translation closely in 1999. No critic connects the book to Triodes (kbgrep 'Bilgames', 'brought him bread': none; Cooke's 'To Pollen' essay mentions Gilgamesh only for a later poem). Clegg (Poetry London, 2015) notes George's translation as the epigraph to To Pollen (2006), not to Triodes.

    Bilgames fells Inanna's haunted willow and makes her throne and bed and his own ball and mallet from it. Prynne's 'to make play for full day' points straight to the ball game. The cosmic tree turns into a trading day ('peak-time / balance of equity scooping up British Sugar'), and the sequence's sugar refiners stand where Inanna's furniture was. With p. 488, this is the second lift from the same Sumerian poem. Book II is thus framed by a Mesopotamian 'netherworld' as well as by Egyptian 'mummy shots'.   466. The Durchgriff ... Imagine any triode as being replaced

    Appleton, Thermionic Vacuum Tubes (from the 1941 edition; Aldous & Appleton from 1952); not confirmed in the 1932 first edition; chapter on the triode: the equivalent diode, and the anode penetration factor Da (German 'Durchgriff'); OL page index n182 source ↗

    It is convenient to imagine any triode as being replaced by an equivalent diode, the anode potential of which produces the same electrical effect in the region near the cathode as the combined effects of anode and grid potentials in the corresponding triode. ... [the] anode penetration factor, and given the symbol Da (German "Durchgriff"). It is a measure of the extent to which the electric field due to ... This reverse penetration factor, which we shall designate by Dk ...

    The title of the sequence takes its technical base from a standard British valve monograph by the Nobel physicist Appleton. Appleton's symbols Da (anode 'Durchgriff') and Dk (reverse penetration factor) also seem to be in the formulae that head Books I and III ('1 + Da +', '+ Dk'). The equivalent-diode device reduces a three-electrode valve to a two-electrode one, and Prynne uses it as the sequence's model of mediation: a third term (the grid; Irene; a lender) whose effect can be 'replaced' by a fictitious potential. He sets the sentence around the financing of Mozambique's sugar rehabilitation, so the grid that controls the current becomes a consortium of lenders: 'Oil to sugar the map beds out'. Prynne shortens 'electrical effect' and 'anode and grid potentials' to 'effect' and 'anode and grid'.

The exact Prynne wording ('imagine any triode as being replaced', 'in the region near the cathode as the combined effects', 'corresponding triode') occurs only in Appleton (IA thermionicvacuum0000appl and thermionicvacuum0000evap). Inside the item, 'Durchgriff' and 'reverse penetration factor ... Dk' are also confirmed. Open Library gives the page as n182.

S (1962), s.v. sabatu Gt, has 'to grasp one another, to quarrel', but only Huehnergard pairs it with mitlukum in one lesson; lesson on the Gt stem (reciprocal and reflexive meanings); glossary s.v. habalum, malakum, sabatum source ↗

    The run is a set of Akkadian verb-stem glosses: a base stem paired with its derived stem. Malakum 'advise' takes the Gt mitlukum 'deliberate'. Sabatum 'seize' takes the reciprocal Gt tisbutum 'grasp one another, quarrel'. Prynne's 'mirror-image sets' names the reciprocal Gt, and 'right at the verbal root' names the triliteral root of Semitic grammar. The page is one of several drawn from Mesopotamian material that Prynne read in 1999 (George's Gilgamesh, pp. 488, 494), and the grammar of reciprocity becomes the boys' quarrel.

    The pediment is a recurring motif of the sequence ('dippy birds ... along the pediment', 'the pediment writes the balcony', 'the cut-open pediments of classical exits'). Here Prynne gives its source in Regency architectural doctrine on the decorum of the orders. Soane's lesson concerns the honour of the sacred form, and Soane goes on to tell how Caesar's house received a pediment by special decree. Prynne follows it with 'Just bring one up on the balcony', so the sacred form becomes a fitting that anyone can install. The same lectures discuss the Attic and the parapet, both of which Triodes uses ('the attic swaps salt for molasses', 'along the parapet the muses gazed').

    These lines take up the title's Tempest source inside the sequence. Prospero's muddy shore here becomes Alonso's wish to lie 'mudded in that oozy bed' with a son he believes drowned. Prynne gives it as a holiday wish to 'chill out by the water line' and sends it into credit idiom: 'Lie on tick'. Lycidas, also an elegy for a drowned youth with 'oozy' locks, is braided into the same lines (see the Lycidas finding). The page thus sets two canonical drownings against one another, and the reasonable shore stays unanswering. 'Oozy bed' alone is a common poetic collocation.

    allusion. The Tempest is known as the source of the title (Will Poole 2006, cited by Lash 2010, pp. 52-3). kbgrep 'oozy', 'mudded', 'tread the ooze': no hits. This verbal borrowing inside the sequence has not been noted.

'to tread the downy turf' three lines later has the frame of Prospero's 'to tread the ooze'. The V.i passage is about 70 lines after Prospero's 'the approaching tide / Will shortly fill the reasonable shore / That now lies foul and muddy', which Poole and Lash take to be the source of the title.

  479. its oozy derelict bed. ... to tread the downy turf. Feel the careful heelprint
    so soft and sprung, twitching this mantle to shew
    willing in turning, not a word left on the plate. [p. 527:] sun again set on fresh glimmer to anticipate     John Milton, Lycidas Unanswering Rational Shore (2001) · Unanswering Rational Shore · l.13009 · p.525 · new/high

    Justa Edouardo King (Cambridge, 1638); Poems of Mr. John Milton (1645); any standard ed., e.g. Poetical Works, ed. H. C. Beeching (Oxford, 1900); ll. 175, 186-193 (also ll. 34, 140, 168); Prynne pp. 525-526 source ↗

    With Nectar pure his oozy Lock's he laves ... Thus sang the uncouth Swain to th'Okes and rills ... And now the Sun had stretch'd out all the hills, / And now was dropt into the Western bay; / At last he rose, and twitch'd his Mantle blew: / To morrow to fresh Woods, and Pastures new. [also l. 34 'Fauns with clov'n heel'; l. 140 'That on the green terf suck the honied showres'; l. 168 'So sinks the day-star in the Ocean bed']

    Lycidas is an elegy for a young man drowned off a 'shore', and it ends with the swain rising in the sunset to go on 'To morrow to fresh Woods'. That ending is the canonical figure of consolation in English pastoral. Prynne keeps the gesture ('twitching this mantle ... willing in turning') but empties it into the idiom of a cleared plate, and he turns 'fresh Woods' into 'fresh glimmer' set to 'anticipate / new tests for old faults'. The elegy's own nearby lines (l. 183, 'Henceforth thou art the Genius of the shore') bear on the title. Milton's diseased flock, 'swoln with wind ... Rot inwardly, and foul contagion spread' (ll. 126-7), also stands behind a page that has 'harvest home', 'ophthalmic lesions' and 'swabbed specimen charges' in the foot-and-mouth year 2001. 'Oozy' is shared with the Tempest, and 'turf' and 'heel' are supporting colour only.

    adaptation. kbgrep 'twitching this mantle', 'downy turf', 'heelprint', 'oozy': no hits. 'Lycidas' occurs in the corpus only in work on other poems (Latter on The English Intelligencer; the Epsians Milton papers). Lash (2010), Grant (2008) and Flores-Bórquez (2007) name Shakespeare, Joyce, O'Hara and Jones Very, not Milton. A web search for Prynne + the title + Lycidas found nothing.

    Verified: Read the full text of Lycidas in the Beeching ed. (Gutenberg #1745). 'twitching this mantle' answers 'twitch'd his Mantle'; it is followed at once by the turn of departure ('willing in turning'), as in Milton's last couplet. The next printed page opens with 'sun again set on fresh glimmer', which takes the sunset of l. 191 and the 'fresh' of l. 193 in the same order. The same page of Prynne also has 'oozy ... bed' (Lycidas 168, 175), 'turf' (l. 140 'terf') and 'heel' (l. 34), all within five lines.

  481. closely levelled out. The ploughshare has been through
    the ground browbeaten guzzle     William Wordsworth, Michael: A Pastoral Poem Acrylic Tips (2002) · Acrylic Tips · l.13152 · p.537 · new/high

    Lyrical Ballads, vol. II (1800); text as in The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, ed. William Knight, vol. 2 (1882-89); closing verse-paragraph, l. 484 (Knight's numbering) source ↗

    at her death the estate / Was sold, and went into a stranger's hand. / The Cottage which was named the EVENING STAR / Is gone--the ploughshare has been through the ground / On which it stood; great changes have been wrought / In all the neighbourhood

    This is the last scene of 'Michael', the founding English pastoral of lost patrimony. Debt (the 'forfeiture' Michael pays as surety) costs the old shepherd his only son, the estate passes 'into a stranger's hand', and the plough wipes out the house. Acrylic Tips is set among the sheep stations of Western Australia and is dedicated to a shearer. Hall reads its plot as a father cut off from his child. Into that setting the borrowing brings both of Michael's losses, the child and the land. 'Levelled out' just before the line describes the razed cottage. The ploughshare passing over the ground of a dwelling also bears on terra nullius: European pastoral treats the ground as empty once the plough has crossed it. The English poem of dispossession is moved into the scene of colonial dispossession.

    quotation. kbgrep 'ploughshare has been through': no hits. 'Michael' appears in the corpus only in Caddy's general list of Wordsworth's walking poems. Matthew Hall, 'Terra Nullius: Colonial Violence in Prynne's Acrylic Tips', JBIIP 8.1 (2016), read in full: he does not mention Wordsworth. Hall reads the poem as pastoral elegy and mentions Kinsella and Hesiod. A web search for Prynne + Acrylic Tips + Michael found nothing.

    Verified: Exhaustive Project Gutenberg 5-word match; read in PG #12145 (Knight ed.) and confirmed in Matthew Arnold, On Translating Homer (PG #65381), which quotes the same lines. Prynne keeps Wordsworth's words in order and breaks his line after 'through', so that 'the ground' begins the next line.

The borrowing therefore puts an actual Aboriginal mourning song, in its anthologised English, inside the dispossession the sequence anatomises: the lament survives only as an object of print transfer, which is itself one of the 'acrylic' questions (Western Desert painting as commodity) the title raises. The 'true bone' at l. 13158 carries the companion Morning Star song into the same stanza.

    Hawkes: 'In my dragon car and chariot on the thunder, / With cloud-banners fluttering upon the wind. / I heave a long sigh as I start ...     The Lord of the East is the sun god. His song follows one day from the glow before dawn, through the chariot ride under cloud-banners and the shot with the long arrow at the Wolf star, to the plunge into darkness at sunset. In two lines Prynne compresses the whole arc: 'my long arrow', the 'perfect glow', the 'cloud banners', and the descent ('final sunk'). He then grounds it at once ('to root there') and surrounds it with a 'pint upgrade' and 'no / furnace'. The shamanic solar journey, from a text that Prynne knew well through his Chinese work, is set near the poem's floodways and canals, a second non-European ritual song beside the Arnhem Land Morning Star song that the poem also uses. Both are songs about a heavenly body that dies and returns.

  487. Burning child says ... to
    dress admonishment ... touch your lips sewn to silence ... Immobile     Sigmund Freud, The Interpretation of Dreams Acrylic Tips (2002) · Acrylic Tips · l.13379 · p.546 · new/medium

    trans. James Strachey, Standard Edition vols IV-V (1953); also A. A. Brill trans. (1913); ch. VII, opening (SE V, 509) source ↗

    the child stood near his bed clasping his arms and calling out reproachfully, 'Father, don't you see that I am burning?' (Brill); 'caught him by the arm and whispered to him reproachfully: "Father, don't you see I'm burning?"' (Strachey); Freud then names it 'the dream of the burning child'

    In Freud's most famous dream, a dead child speaks a reproach to the father who failed to keep watch while the candles burned the body. Prynne's burning child also 'says', and what it says comes as 'admonishment'. The words around it fit the scene: 'Immobile', 'lips sewn to silence', and 'day care who does', which asks who is keeping watch. This supports Hall's account of a father separated from his child, and it makes the poem's last page a waking to a reproach that comes too late. The confidence is medium because the two words 'burning child' are the only verbal contact, but the reproach is a thematic contact as well.

Carol Watts, Sitegeist 8 (2012), reads late Prynne through Laplanche and was not checked for the burning-child dream.

    In Ockham's chapter, 'property' (proprium) is a logical predicable: a predicate that belongs to every member of a species and to that species only. The logical rule that a property is tied to its subject becomes the question of who owns what, and on whose terms the trade-law regime gives anything out.

    echo. Pietrzak notes the poem's 'hand on hand proverb' and its proverbial idiom but does not trace the Latin.

    Verified: The proverb is standard. Its Latin sources are cited from general knowledge, and I did not open the texts in this session.

  490. a security of everlasting triumph Percy Bysshe Shelley, Laon and Cythna / The Revolt of Islam, Preface Biting the Air (2003) · Biting the Air · l.13613 · p.561 · new/high

    Preface to Laon and Cythna (1817), reprinted as The Revolt of Islam (1818); in any Complete Poetical Works (e.g. ed. Hutchinson, Oxford, 1904; Project Gutenberg #4800); Preface, paragraph on the French Revolution and Malthus source ↗

    Metaphysics, and inquiries into moral and political science, have become little else than vain attempts to revive exploded superstitions, or sophisms like those of Mr. Malthus, calculated to lull the oppressors of mankind into a security of everlasting triumph. Our works of fiction and poetry have been overshadowed by the same infectious gloom.

    The lift sits in the indented column of p.561, between 'deficit, slippage' and 'gravitate to the entrance be steady indigent'. For Shelley the phrase names what Malthus's population doctrine does: it tells the powerful that the misery of the poor is natural law, so their dominion is safe for ever. Biting the Air writes in the idiom of the WTO and the pharmaceutical patent ('patent lockage', 'parallel imports under licence', 'demographic twitch', 'sessional poverty values'). There the Malthusian sophism comes back as trade and health economics, which ration life-saving supply and call the result 'security'. The stanza ends 'waiting to be born'. That changes Shelley's own hope, that mankind is 'emerging from their trance' in a 'slow, gradual, silent change', into a toxic birth. The letter to Riley shows that Prynne thought 36 years earlier that Shelley's anti-Malthus prose must be rewritten for the age of demography. This poem appears to carry out that programme.

    quotation. kbgrep finds nothing for 'everlasting triumph', 'Revolt of Islam' or 'Laon and Cythna'. Web search for Prynne + phrase found nothing. Pietrzak (Levity of Design, 2012) and Potts (Guardian, 2005) read this stanza as WTO/GATT, pharmaceutical and Yeatsian, and do not mention Shelley. Corroboration: in a letter to Peter Riley (13 Sept 1967) Prynne copies out Shelley's attack on Malthus from A Philosophical View of Reform, and says that its pathos must be rewritten now with the sophistication of birth control and modern demography and the sophistry of current welfare economics.

    Verified: inside.py: 261 hits, all Shelley or quoting it (Webb 1977, Child's British Poets 1864, Woodings 1968). Read in full in PG #4800. A 4-gram match of the whole poem against Shelley's verse and prose (PG 4800, 5428, 67925-6; the 1920 Philosophical View of Reform) finds only this run.

  492. Reaching colloid to serve, cleft for me. Augustus Montague Toplady, 'Rock of Ages, cleft for me' Blue Slides at Rest (2004) · Blue Slides at Rest · l.13762 · p.568 · new/medium

    The hymn's opening, which asks for shelter in the riven rock, closes a sentence of laboratory diction ('colloid'). The next clause, 'Hurt no one in durance', continues in a devotional register.     echo. kbgrep 'cleft for me', 'Toplady': no hits.

  493. for ever the blue
    sky bends fluently over all wand purchased     Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Christabel Blue Slides at Rest (2004) · Blue Slides at Rest · l.13820 · p.570 · new/high

    Complete Poetical Works, ed. E. H. Coleridge (Oxford, 1912); Part I, ll. 329-31 (E. H. Coleridge numbering) source ↗

    But this she knows, in joys and woes, / That saints will aid if men will call: / For the blue sky bends over all!

    Prynne keeps Coleridge's line almost whole and inserts 'fluently', so that the sky's protective bend becomes a fluent motion. In Coleridge the line closes Part I with the narrator's assurance that heaven protects the sleeping Christabel, even while she lies in the arms of Geraldine, 'the worker of these harms', who seems to slumber 'As a mother with her child'. That scene of an endangered girl in a false mother's arms suits the sequence's concern with the infant and its carers. Prynne's sentence goes on to 'wand purchased', which makes the protection look bought or conjured. The 'for' in 'for ever' keeps Coleridge's 'For'.

    adaptation. kbgrep 'blue sky bends' and 'Christabel': no hits in the Prynne corpus.

    Verified: Read in PG #29090 (Coleridge, Complete Poetical Works), Christabel, Conclusion to Part I, ll. 279-331.

  494. Downy finish is

    'The swan's road into Palestine' is five words, verbatim, from Bradley's prose Elene. In that poem Constantine's mother Helena sails to the Holy Land to make the Jews give up the buried True Cross. The poem is a story of a woman who 'asks after' a buried thing, and Prynne's 'hers to ask after' keeps that inquest. 'Not yet level' turns the kenning into a road that is still rough. A further link of 'Arms lifted up' to the three crosses lifted from the earth is conjecture.

    quotation. kbgrep "swan's road": only Pietrzak's quotation of the Prynne line, with no source. kbgrep 'Elene' finds only Marriott's 1993 thesis on early Prynne (an unrelated listing of Cynewulf's poems). No Bradley or Cynewulf citation for this poem.

    Verified: inside.py 'the swan's road into Palestine' before 2005: one hit only, Bradley's translation. olinside.py gives the scan page n630. I searched inside the item for 'lifted up', 'Greeks', 'bridle' and saw the Elene context.

  495. Arms lifted up light tremor, gaze tidal to
    average miss finish Greek fire. Floor affecting she
    knows he'll go, white span day breaks in the eastern
    sky, not indie not critical. On micro grassy shelters     Kanze Motomasa (attrib.), trans.     Tokyo: Nippon Gakujutsu Shinkokai, 1955; Rutland, Vt. and Tokyo: Charles E. Tuttle, 1960 and reprints; end of Sumidagawa (play begins p. 143; ending at scan leaf n244 of the 1960 printing) source ↗

    [stage direction] [the Mother] attempts to embrace it, but as the Ghost retreats again into the mound, the Mother falls, clasping the empty air. Rising again she approaches the mound, gazing at the willow-[tree] [...] The vision fades and reappears / And stronger grows her yearning. / Day breaks in the eastern sky. / The ghost has vanished; / What seemed her boy / Is but a grassy mound / Lost on the wide, desolate moor. / Sadness and tender pity fill all hearts

    The passage tracks the climax of Sumidagawa, the Noh play behind Curlew River: the mother tries to embrace her dead son's ghost, falls ('Floor affecting'), rises and gazes, the ghost withdraws ('she / knows he'll go'), 'Day breaks in the eastern sky', and what seemed her boy 'Is but a grassy mound' (Prynne's 'micro grassy shelters'). The verbatim clause is short and the rest is a sequence of gestures, hence medium confidence, but the order of events matches and the poem already uses Plomer's English version at l. 13962. Prynne thus reaches behind Britten's Christian parable (where the boy's spirit promises resurrection) to the Buddhist original, where dawn simply dissolves the vision into grass, and the 'not critical' flatness answers that ending. 'Arms lifted up' answers the stage direction where the Mother, 'with outstretched arms ... runs towards it, and attempts to embrace it'. Sumidagawa is the Noh play on which Britten and Plomer based Curlew River (see l. 13962).

    adaptation. kbgrep 'Sumidagawa', 'Sumida', 'Umewaka', 'Nippon Gakujutsu', 'day breaks in the eastern': no hits. The Curlew River finding (hunt-a) already identifies the Britten parable, which Plomer based on Sumidagawa, in the closing pages; the Noh original itself has not been noted.

    Verified: inside.py 'day breaks in the eastern sky' (before 2005) gives 11 hits, of which the only non-trivial cluster is this translation of Sumidagawa (Noh Drama 1960; quoted in Malm 1986 and others). I searched inside nohdrama0000niho for 'the ghost has vanished', 'grassy', 'mound', 'clasping the empty air', 'Rising again', 'desolate moor', 'Sumida', 'lost' and saw each snippet. I also searched inside the Curlew River libretto (curlewriver0000unse) for 'eastern sky', 'day breaks', 'dawn', 'mound', 'vanished', 'the ghost': none of the dawn or mound wording is there, so the line comes from the Noh translation, not from Plomer.

  496. Search lamp
    party cress-market begins, long before daylight bites
    like boiling water race blue naked feet.     Henry Mayhew, London Labour and the London Poor, vol. 1 Blue Slides at Rest (2004) · Blue Slides at Rest · l.13911 · p.572 · new/high

    London, 1851 (enlarged edn 1861-62; Dover facsimile 1968); the passage is also reprinted in Peter Quennell (ed.), Mayhew's London (1949/1951) and in Augustus Mayhew, Paved with Gold (1858); 'Of Watercress-Selling, in Farringdon-Market' (section on the street-sellers of green stuff) source ↗

    As winter draws near, the Farringdon cress-market begins long before daylight. [...] Before him is an opened hamper, with a candle fixed in the centre of the bright green cresses [...] 'Ah! Mrs. Dolland,' cried the saleswoman in a gracious tone, 'can you keep yourself warm? it bites the fingers like biling water, it do.' [...] the children crying, as their naked feet were trodden upon [...] A sickly-looking boy, of about five, whose head just reached above the hampers, now crept forward, treading with his blue naked feet over the cold stones as a cat does over wet ground.

    Prynne takes three separate details from one paragraph of Mayhew: the opening sentence, the saleswoman's 'it bites [...] like biling water', and the five-year-old with 'blue naked feet'. He joins them into one run-on line, so that the cold daylight 'bites' the children's feet. Reading 'Search lamp' as the candle that lights each hamper in the dark market is interpretation. The lift puts the destitute child of mid-Victorian street trade, the barefoot cress-seller, at the centre of the sequence's late pages about a mother, a child, debt, and custody. The section is about the 'very poorest of the poor', and children 'deserted by their parents'. Prynne's own 'child shelf', 'low rent' and 'loan' in the first poems are a modern version of the same economy.

    adaptation. kbgrep 'cress-market' finds only Pietrzak, Levity of Design (2012), ch. 4, who quotes 'Search lamp / party cress-market begins' and reads it as a mother escaping from hospital, with no source. kbgrep 'Mayhew', 'Farringdon', 'London Labour', 'biling water', 'blue naked feet': no Prynne-related hit. Prynne knew Mayhew: in a letter to Dorn of 20 Dec. 1963 he says he has ordered vol. IV of London Labour for himself and for Dorn.

    Verified: Exhaustive Project Gutenberg 6-word match (bsr-pg-candidates.tsv); read the full passage in PG #55998; the same text appears in Mayhew's London (IA mayhewslondon0000mayh, scan p. n604). All three Prynne clauses come from one page of Mayhew, in order.

    First of all my lord went away from his people here / over the tossing waves; I was sleepless with anxiety, / not knowing in what land my prince might be. / Then, on account of my woeful need, I went forth, / a friendless wretch, to seek service. [...] our love is now / as if it never had been. Far and near I must endure / the enmity of my dearly beloved. / I was bidden dwell in the cave in the earth / under the oak-tree in the forest grove. [...] while I at dawn walk alone / under the oak-tree through these caves in the earth. [...] my disconsolate lord, sits under a rocky cliff, / covered with sleet by the storm, encompassed by water / in a hall of sorrow.

    Two pages of the closing sequence are threaded with Mackie's prose translation of the Old English 'Wife's Lament': the abandoned wife 'sleepless with anxiety, not knowing' where her lord is (Prynne's 'sleepless with / anxiety unknowing', which Pietrzak took for the Cloud of Unknowing), her 'woeful need', the 'Far and near' enmity she must endure, her exile 'bidden dwell in the cave in the earth' and walking 'through these caves in the earth', and the lord 'encompassed by water' (Prynne's 'encompassed by floods'). 'Trim forward but as it never was' (l. 13918) and 'cut down as had never' (l. 13986) may also bend Mackie's 'as if it never had been'. With the source, the woman of these pages is an exile under compulsion ('bidden'), kept in an earth-dwelling by others' plotting, which sits with the care/wardship law and Curlew River already found here: a separated woman whose grief is ordered and housed by authority. It also confirms that Prynne was reading Old English verse in translation for this book (cf. Bradley's Elene for 'the swan's road into Palestine').

'sleepless with anxiety, not knowing' returns only the two Mackie copies; 'these caves in the earth' returns Mackie and Diamond's Old English Grammar (a different version: 'through these caves in the earth. (37) There I may sit'), so Prynne's 'bidden dwell' fixes the Mackie version. 'encompassed by floods' (Prynne) has 5 unrelated hits.

  498. warm and bright to end as
    dust by the road, risen child unspeaking by human hand     William Plomer (libretto) and Benjamin Britten, Curlew River: A Parable for Church Performance Blue Slides at Rest (2004) · Blue Slides at Rest · l.13962 · p.574 · new/high

    London: Faber Music, 1964 (libretto); the libretto is also printed in Patricia Howard, The Operas of Benjamin Britten (1969); the Madwoman at the tomb, near the end (libretto p. [33]) source ↗

    Madwoman: [...] Did I give birth to him / To have him stolen / And carried far away, / Here to the Eastern Fens / To end as dust by the road? / O, good people, open up the tomb [...] Spirit (off): Go your way in peace, mother. / The dead shall rise again [...] (Ferryman, earlier:) The Heathen said he'd bought him as a slave. The boy said nothing. [...] (Madwoman:) My only child was lost, / Seized as a slave / By a stranger, a foreigner.

    The words 'to end as dust by the road' come from the climax of Britten's church parable. The Madwoman, who has wandered east to look for her son, learns that a stranger took him as a slave, and that he died by the road and was buried by the river. A line later Prynne's 'risen child' answers the Spirit of the Boy, who rises from the tomb and sings 'The dead shall rise again'. Prynne's child is 'unspeaking', which returns to the Ferryman's 'The boy said nothing' and takes the consolation away. 'Rankle against a stranger' and 'foreign outland' (ll. 13979-80) may recall Plomer's 'a stranger, a foreigner'. With Britten as a source, the final pages of the sequence read as the story of a demented mother who has lost a child taken by strangers. That is the plot Pietrzak reconstructs without a source.

  499. Claiming up
    tender placement not recoverable for grief or sorrow yield
    to dictates value this loss yielded, bond consortium make
    a twilled mouth shut. Give outright. Yet minor exempted     Court of Appeal, F. v. Wirral Metropolitan Borough Council Blue Slides at Rest (2004) · Blue Slides at Rest · l.13973 · p.575 · new/high

    [1991] Fam 69; [1991] 2 WLR 1132; [1991] 2 All ER 648; All ER 1991 vol. 2, scan p. n986 source ↗

    the proposition that 'while damages are recoverable in respect of nervous shock they are not recoverable for grief or sorrow'. (WLR 1991 vol. 2, quoting Hinz v Berry:) In English law no damages are awarded for grief or sorrow caused by a person's death. (Same volume, F. v. Wirral MBC:) the rights, said to belong to parents, to enjoy consortium, in the widest sense, with their children [...] a parent has any right in his natural child, interference with which would give rise to [...]

    The five-word legal formula fixes the register of the stanza. The topic is the English rule that grief has no money value: you can claim for 'nervous shock' or 'bereavement', but not for grief or sorrow. 'Consortium' (the loss-of-society claim), 'minor', 'loss', 'claiming', 'placement', and on the next page 'the natural child', 'In care' and 'strong wardship' are all terms from family and fatal-accident law. These words recast the mourning mother of the closing elegy as a claimant whose sorrow the law rules not recoverable. The source is the doctrine as reported, not one judgment that I could pin down. The case is a mother's claim for damages after her children were placed in care with foster parents, which accounts for 'tender placement', 'consortium', 'natural child', 'In care' and 'wardship' together.

    adaptation. kbgrep 'grief or sorrow': no hit. Pietrzak (2012) paraphrases the passage as a 'bond consortium' rejecting a father's claim, with no legal source.

    Verified: inside.py 'not recoverable for grief or sorrow' (no year limit) returns exactly 2 texts, both 1991 law reports. I searched inside bwb_KV-026-915_2 for 'consortium', 'natural child', 'placement', 'wardship', 'Hillsborough' and saw the snippets. I read the Fatal Accidents Act s. 1A text on legislation.gov.uk. I could not identify which judgment the All ER quotation comes from.
